text:
Volvo Cars executives this week shared their automotive outlook with investors, and the broader picture was a bleak assessment of how geopolitics, trade, and tariffs are fundamentally changing what is now a fully global auto industry. But the best solution for tough times is the same as it's always been: new product.

The Swedish automaker promises a bevy of new vehicles, including region-specific vehicles for Western markets and China, all coming by 2030, representing Volvo Cars' largest product offensive ever.

Volvo Platforms For The West, Shared Platforms For China

While we wait for more details about these new vehicles, it appears they will all come with a cord, either as fully battery-electric models or as next-generation plug-in hybrids with bigger electric motors for longer EV range. Volvo is planning 13 in total, an ambitious number to launch in less than four years.

Among the "new and regionally tailored cars" are seven earmarked for Western markets. These will spring from Volvo's SPA2 and SPA3 platforms, which means cost savings in technology and manufacturing and improved profitability, said Volvo Cars CEO and President Håkan Samuelsson, who also calls these cars "100% Volvo,"developed in Sweden.

Meanwhile, Volvo and its owner, China's Geely Holding Group, will collaborate on six new vehicles intended only for China by using shared platforms and "a software stack for China as well as common parts and a common supply chain." While many automakers fear Chinese encroachment in their markets, Samuelsson sees Volvo's relationship with Geely as a distinct advantage in an auto industry now in severe turmoil.

Wasn't Globalization A Good Idea?

Samuelsson recalled how, years ago, auto executives embraced globalization as a strategy to "build one car in one factory and sell it everywhere." But times have changed. "In the text book, it could be a good idea," he told investors. "It worked some years ago. It is not going to work in the future." Now, trade disputes, lethal military conflicts, and general economic uncertainty are forcing automakers to establish different strategies for different regions, with more interaction with customers, he said.​​​​​​​

"If we thought we had tough competition in the car industry, just wait – it will be even tougher," Samuelsson said, noting the Chinese market, though enormous, cannot absorb all the cars produced domestically, due to severe overcapacity.

"When you can't sell them domestically, what do you think they will do? They will, of course, export them. Americans have closed the door. The rest of us have to take it, and South America has very low tariffs, so they're first on the list. Hyper-competition will come."

–Håkan Samuelsson, Volvo Cars CEO and President

Volvo Has An EV Hit On Its Hands

Despite the big-picture concerns, Volvo appears to be defying the odds in demonstrating real growth in the battery-electric vehicle market outside of China. In Europe, Volvo holds 2.3% of the overall car market, while Germany's biggest luxury players – BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Audi – each hover around 5.5%.

Within the BEV market itself, Volvo claims about 4% of that segment, but that figure doesn't include the all-new 2027 EX60 electric crossover. Factor in the retail orders for the new EX60, and Volvo's EV share in Europe goes well past 5%, in line with the German luxury brands, said Erik Severinson, Volvo's chief commercial officer.

"On the BEV market in Europe right now with what we're selling with the EX60, Volvo has roughly the same market share as the premium Germans have, which we never, ever have been close to in the past."

–Erik Severinson, Volvo Chief Commercial Officer

Fuel Prices Driving Up Euro EV Sales

Severinson also provided data (above) showing how rapidly the EV market has grown in China and particularly in Germany, especially as fuel prices there have skyrocketed in recent months in response to the war in the Middle East. In Germany, Severinson said EV sales now account for 25% of all vehicles sold in Europe's largest market.

"Actually in the last weeks, almost 50% of all new cars sold in Germany are fully electric," Severinson said. "So Germany is going electric and Germany is massively important for the European car market." Germany exports a lot of used cars to other markets in Europe. "So when Germany turns, a lot of other markets will follow as well."

CarBuzz Insight – Why This Matters:

Of course, US consumers are also feeling pain at the pump, but they aren't responding by flocking to EVs, like they are in Germany. "Fully electric cars have actually gone down in the last few months," Severinson said of the US. Still, Volvo is convinced that across the auto industry and all powertrain configurations, "electrification is the path to grow, and the only thing that is growing is cars with a cord."

A Wind Turbine By Any Other Name So, what is this Integrated Energy Systems Office?

What’s up with the US Department of Energy these days? Over the past few weeks, the agency’s website has been reposting, recirculating, or updating Biden-era information about renewable energy. The PR blitz also includes brand new developments like PacWave South, a major clean energy facility that finally opened for business on August 27 after a years-long effort. Even wind turbines are coming in for their share of attention, which is remarkable considering US President Donald Trump’s longstanding, fetishistic animosity towards wind power.

The War On Wind Turbines

To be clear, it would be silly to expect DOE to launch any new funding program that helps the US wind industry get back on its feet after going through the Trump chopper. In particular, Trump has zeroed in on offshore wind, even to the extent of rewarding — some say bribing — offshore lease holders to walk away from their plans.

Still, among the web pages recently updated by the Energy Department is an explainer titled, “Wind Manufacturing and Supply Chain.” Dated September 10, 2026, the page starts off by explaining that DOE “works with wind energy technology suppliers to promote advanced manufacturing capabilities. The goals are to increase reliability while lowering production costs and promote an industry that can meet all demands domestically while competing in the global market.”

“The Integrated Energy Systems Office supports industry partnerships and targeted R&D funding that integrate new designs, materials, and processes into manufacturing facilities, thus making energy technologies more affordable,” DOE adds somewhat mysteriously.

A Wind Turbine By Any Other Name

So, what is this Integrated Energy Systems Office? The Wind Manufacturing and Supply Chain explainer was posted under the IESO heading, and therein lies a tale.

On September 17, DOE blasted out an email explaining that IESO is a new office that combines the former Solar Energy Technologies Office and Wind Energy Technologies Office into, well, one office.

“Our core mission at IESO is to enhance grid reliability and resilience, secure U.S. technological leadership across diverse energy generation sources, and lower energy costs for hardworking Americans,” DOE states.

“By combining our efforts, we can more effectively seize the incredible opportunities presented by the evolving energy landscape to unleash American energy dominance,” DOE adds for good measure.

If that language sounds familiar, that’s because DOE routinely lauds fossil fuels for the same reasons. So, take that with a Texas-sized grain of salt. It really is beyond belief that the Trump administration would release any funding in support of the wind industry, unless, of course, forced to do so by court order.

Still, a brand new word popped up in the IESO email, which makes things rather interesting. In accord with its combined solar-plus-wind mission, IESO lists advanced photovoltaics, solar thermal technologies, cybersecurity and other grid integration systems, and permitting under its wing, along with something called “aeromechanical energy systems.”

Aeromechanical energy systems! Now, that’s a word combo you don’t see every day, especially when something more simple and readable will do, like “wind turbines.”

Apparently someone forgot to read their Strunk and White. Be that as it may, IESO tasks the Aeromechanical Energy Systems branch with addressing “challenges to the long-term reliability and performance of wind energy systems” and facilitating “the recycling of end-of-life wind energy components.”

Where Are These Aeromechanical Energy Systems Of Which You Speak?

Further muddying the waters for any kind of wind industry support, IESO comes under the organizational chart of the recently established Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation.

Apparently OCMEI put the IESO cart before the horse. The new IESO web page lists only one open funding opportunity and exactly zero upcoming opportunities, followed by a list of programs “under review.” Other than that, the IESO website is barely populated.

For the record, the only open funding opportunity is directed at the booming space solar field. All of the programs listed for review also come under the solar umbrella or other general grid initiatives.

The Fight For Onshore Wind Power Continues

A quick glance at DOE’s other open funding programs does reveal considerable activity on the part of CMEI covering energy resources in general. Some of that background noise may benefit the wind industry, eventually. As for the here and now, don’t expect to see any fresh round of funding opportunities in the “aeromechanical energy systems” field any time soon.

In the meantime, Trump’s war on wind power continues. Last year a federal judge affirmed that the President — any President — can stop issuing new offshore wind leases, which pretty much stifles further growth because virtually all offshore lease opportunities fall under federal jurisdiction.

Still, the same judge, and a series of other judges, ruled that Trump has no authority to delay or stop work on offshore wind projects that already have leases in hand. That explains the series of offshore lease buyouts/briberies. It’s a last, desperate attempt to stop any more wind turbines from going into the water under Trump’s watch.

The Hail Mary attempt may ultimately fail, as a group of coastal states has sued to reverse the transactions. Some members of Congress have also alleged that the buyouts were illegally funneled through the Department of Justice.

As for the onshore wind industry, at first glance there is much wiggle room for wind turbines to spring up, if not on land owned by the federal government then on land that falls under private, state, or local ownership. Or not, as the case may be. Last year, The US Department of Defense froze a heretofore routine process for reviewing wind farm permits.

The review process, which also includes the Federal Aviation Administration, applies to projects with wind turbines more than 200 feet tall. In July of this year, a group of 19 state attorneys general sued the Trump administration to get things moving again.

“In August 2025, DoD abruptly stopped following this process. Officials ceased countersigning mitigation agreements, stopped sending completed agreements to developers for signature, and delayed or halted communications with developers about mitigation,” explains one member of the group, Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown.

In August of this year, a federal judge agreed and ruled that the freeze was illegal. Shocker! Of course, the Trump administration could always find new ways to block new wind farms, and reportedly it has. Still, US Presidents come and go, but the wind blows forever…

text:
By Joyce Lee

Sept 18 (Reuters) - South Korea and the United States are finalising the implementation of Seoul's pledged $350 billion investment package under a trade deal struck last year that lowered US tariffs on South Korean goods to 15%.

Out of the $350 billion, $150 billion ‌is earmarked for shipbuilding with details still being worked out for the remaining $200 billion in strategic investments.

Below are details of the ‌projects under discussion, according to media reports and a South Korean lawmaker, although the country's industry ministry has said details have not been set.

TEXAS GAS-FIRED POWER PLANT

The first project is a combined-cycle ​gas power plant in Encinal, Texas.

The 6.3 gigawatt project aims to supply electricity to AI data centres and semiconductor plants in Texas.

To reduce risk, the project is expected to be developed in stages, starting with 1.4 GW of gas turbine facilities, before later adding 4.9 GW of combined-cycle facilities, according to multiple South Korean media outlets, including JoongAng Ilbo.

The two sides agreed on investment of around $22.3 billion, and the use of a bilateral special-purpose investment vehicle going forward, the ‌reports said.

EIGHT NUCLEAR REACTORS, WESTINGHOUSE STAKE

Seoul and Washington ⁠are discussing the construction of up to eight large nuclear reactors in the United States.

At about $15 billion per reactor, the nuclear sector could account for a significant portion of the investment package, according to the Korea Economic Daily newspaper ⁠and other outlets.

The two countries are negotiating for six reactors to use technology from US company Westinghouse and two using a South Korean design.

If built, the South Korean-designed units would be the first Korean reactors in the United States.

Separately, Seoul is negotiating to acquire a stake in US nuclear company Westinghouse. South Korea sought around ​a ​15% stake to gain a board seat, but the US offered only 5% to ​10%, media reports said.

The value of the investment would ‌depend on Westinghouse's valuation ahead of a planned initial public offering, but could amount to $15 billion to $20 billion, implying a 15% stake could be worth $2.25 billion to $3 billion, according to Korea Economic Daily.

Westinghouse's stock is currently held by Canadian asset manager Brookfield and its partners with 51% and Canadian uranium miner Cameco with 49%.

ALASKA LNG PROJECT

Another project under discussion is South Korean participation in the Alaska liquefied natural gas project, a long-stalled pipeline and export scheme championed by US President Donald Trump.

The Alaska LNG development estimated to be worth $44 billion would transport gas drilled from northern Alaska via a 1,300-km (807 miles) ‌pipeline to Nikiski, for export to Asian countries.

South Korea has approached the plan cautiously ​and Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan told parliament last November that Alaska LNG was a "high-risk business".

South ​Korean media has said Seoul has sought to include the Alaska ​LNG project in the US investment memorandum without a binding commitment.

NUCLEAR FUEL REPROCESSING

A fourth potential investment concerns Washington seeking ‌South Korean support on reprocessing spent nuclear fuel, according to ​South Korean ruling party lawmaker Yoon Hu-duk.

The ​US is linking this proposal to South Korea's push to build nuclear-powered submarines and secure fuel, Yonhap news agency said.

The United States has proposed a project involving processing 4,000 tons of spent nuclear fuel, the lawmaker said.

At a leaders' summit last November, the two countries ​agreed on a joint factsheet in which Washington approved South ‌Korean plans to build a nuclear-powered submarine and to work closely with Seoul on fuel procurement.

CARBON CAPTURE

A fifth potential project involves ​carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), according to South Korean lawmaker Yoon.

This is an area where major US energy firms have ​already attracted large-scale investment.

(Reporting by Joyce LeeEditing by Ed Davies and Shri Navaratnam)

title: DOE's New Strategic Plan Sets an Expansive Course for Energy Dominance Financing
description:

text:
The US Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF), recently rebranded from the former Loan Programs Office (LPO), released its Strategic Plan for 2026–2030. The Plan outlines an agenda to deploy federal financing in support of five principal goals:

reducing energy costs;

adding firm generation capacity;

advancing energy innovation, domestic technologies, and domestic manufacturing;

strengthening supply chain security; and

creating high-quality American jobs.

The five goals are set against three challenges:

energy affordability in the face of unprecedented demand,

aging and underinvested infrastructure that is threatening grid reliability, and

the need to secure domestic supply chains and win the AI race.

Although EDF represents a significant reorientation of the former LPO, its emphasis on commercial deployment, infrastructure investment, and disciplined federal lending preserves continuity with the predecessor organization.

Expanded Loan Authority and Investment Priorities

Central to the strategic plan are EDF’s authorities. The 2025 reconciliation law — commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and described by DOE as the Working Families Tax Cut — substantially amended Section 1706, replacing the former Energy Infrastructure Reinvestment Program with the Energy Dominance Financing Program. The revised authority broadens eligibility to encompass energy and critical minerals infrastructure, projects that increase the capacity or output of operating facilities, and projects that provide electricity needed to maintain grid reliability or system adequacy. In addition to Section 1706, EDF administers the Section 1703 Energy Financing Program, the Advanced Technology Vehicles Manufacturing Loan Program, and the Tribal Energy Financing Program. Together, these four loan programs have more than $300 billion in combined authority. EDF also manages the separate $2.5 billion Transmission Facilitation Program revolving fund, which can use capacity contracts and other arrangements to reduce the risks associated with major transmission projects.

In total, EDF has more than $300 billion in combined loan authority across four different programs. According to the plan, EDF intends to pursue “hundreds of billions” of dollars in new financing commitments through 2030 while maintaining rigorous underwriting and protecting taxpayer interests.

The EDF goals reflect a significant broadening of the federal energy financing mission. While the former LPO was often associated with innovative clean energy technologies, EDF is placing greater emphasis on nuclear energy, hydrocarbons, coal technologies, critical minerals and materials, transmission, utilities, geothermal energy, and manufacturing. Innovation, principally supported under Section 1703, nevertheless remains an important element of EDF’s mission and preserves the office’s long-standing role as a bridge to bankability for emerging energy technologies. Nuclear energy, in particular, is identified as a priority technology capable of advancing EDF’s firm-generation and grid-reliability goals. Nuclear energy’s carbon-free attributes could also broaden support for EDF’s nuclear investments among policymakers focused on emissions reduction. Other technologies, including long-duration energy storage, may similarly align reliability objectives with broader energy policy goals.

Another positive takeaway from the Strategic Plan is the inclusion of the ATVM program. Originally intended for only light-duty vehicles and components, ATVM authorities were expanded under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) to include medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, ships and other maritime vessels, aircraft, and locomotives. The administration’s FY 2027 budget request rescinded approximately $2.3 billion in unobligated ATVM credit-subsidy funding, and provided no new FY 2027 loan-subsidy funding, signaling the possible phase-out of underwriting for new ATVM projects. The ATVM authorities can provide significant support for administration manufacturing objectives, however, and with Congress having the ultimate say on appropriations, there is the potential to see this program more widely utilized.

What Prospective Applicants Should Know

The plan preserves EDF’s emphasis on rigorous underwriting and responsible stewardship of taxpayer funds. Competitive applications should present credible sources of repayment, meaningful sponsor support, realistic construction schedules, and a clear explanation of why EDF financing is necessary to advance the project.

For prospective applicants, the plan provides a clear indication of the projects EDF will prioritize. Some questions may remain about details such as annual financing targets, sector allocations, and how application timelines will be managed, but the overall message is clear: EDF intends to operate as an active strategic lender and to use its substantial federal financing authority to rebuild the nation’s energy and industrial foundation at scale. text:
Hysata to scale UOW clean energy innovation with $49M ARENA funding

Port Kembla facility will turn University of Wollongong hydrogen research into commercial-scale manufacturing

University of Wollongong (UOW) has congratulated Hysata on receiving up to $49 million from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) to establish a commercial-scale manufacturing line for its UOW-developed electrolyser technology at Port Kembla.

The $98 million project will establish a 50 megawatt per annum manufacturing line, with capacity to scale to 200 megawatts per annum as demand grows. The project is expected to create around 40 new manufacturing, engineering and technical jobs in the Illawarra.

UOW Vice-Chancellor and President Professor G.Q. Max Lu AO said the investment was an important milestone in the journey from university research to Australian-made clean-energy technology.

"Hysata's electrolyser started as research in UOW laboratories, and it will now be manufactured at commercial scale a few kilometres down the road at Port Kembla. That is what a research university in a region like ours is for.

"I congratulate the Hysata team on this investment, and I thank Minister Chris Bowen, Minister Tim Ayres and the Member for Cunningham, Alison Byrnes, for backing innovation and advanced manufacturing in the Illawarra.

"Around 40 skilled jobs will be created here, in a region that has been making things for a century and knows how to do it. Discoveries like this take years of patient investment in fundamental research - and partners willing to build on it. Today shows why both matter.

- Vice-Chancellor and President Professor G.Q. Max Lu AO

Developed from research originating at UOW, Hysata’s capillary-fed electrolyser technology is designed to produce renewable hydrogen using less electricity than conventional electrolysers, with applications including steelmaking, chemicals, shipping and heavy transport.

The Port Kembla project will also include early commercial-scale electrolyser deployments and local manufacturing of key components, including membranes, anodes and cathodes. Hysata expects to spend $20 million to $30 million each year with Australian suppliers, supporting the development of a regional clean technology manufacturing ecosystem.

UOW will work with Hysata and TAFE NSW Illawarra on training, internships and skills development pathways to help build the local workforce required to support the clean energy transition.

The funding is being provided through ARENA’s Future Made in Australia Innovation Fund, with Hysata matching the $49 million grant through private capital.

Hysata’s technology was developed from research at UOW and has subsequently progressed through commercialisation and investment to become a globally focused clean technology company.

text:
When it was announced in 2024 that Amplify Cell Technologies would build a $1.9-billion electric vehicle battery plant in Marshall County, Mississippi leaders heralded it as one of the state’s largest economic development projects ever and approved up to $482 million in state incentives.

“This historic investment by these industry-leading companies will enshrine our state at the forefront of the automotive industry for years to come and create 2,000 good-paying jobs in the process,” Gov. Tate Reeves said.

But production, originally slated to start in 2027, is now delayed indefinitely. This is after the state has spent at least $107 million on the project.

However, state economic development leaders say the company hasn’t defaulted on any terms of the agreement for incentives yet.

“The joint venture partners agreed to finish building out the facility while delaying the timing for installing the manufacturing capacity. At this time, the production start date is uncertain,” Cummins, one of the partners in Amplify, announced during its first-quarter earnings call in May. The company attributed the decision to changing demand in the market.

Almost four months later, the company could not share a timeline for when production would start.

“The production timeline is being adjusted to reflect today’s market environment. We thus have no additional information to share at this time,” a representative for Daimler Trucks, another partner in Amplify, told Mississippi Today on Tuesday.

A series of delays

The May announcement is just the latest project setback.

Initially, the company said production would begin in 2027, but in October 2025 the company pushed the start of production to 2028. Then in April, the company laid off 73 of a total of 100 employees at the Byhalia factory.

This is a change from a year ago when the company was celebrating hiring 100 employees and then-CEO Kel Kearns told the Memphis Business Journal that the project was on schedule for production in late 2027.

The Mississippi Development Authority said the company remains in compliance with its contractual obligations with the state for the taxpayer-funded incentives.

According to the memorandum of understanding between the state and the company, Amplify has until 2031 to create 2,000 jobs and make a $1.9-billion investment. If the company fails to meet its contractual obligations, it could have to repay the state up to $232 million.

“MDA has determined that Amplify Cell remains in compliance with its contractual obligations. Should that status change, the agency will take appropriate action consistent with the agreement,” MDA said in April. The agency confirmed on Wednesday that the statement is still accurate.

Incentives for a ‘historic investment’

In 2024, Reeves called the project the “single largest payroll commitment of any major project and the second-largest economic development project.”

At the time, the joint venture between Cummins, Daimler Trucks and PAACAR aimed to be one of the largest commercial battery cell manufacturing companies in the U.S.

During a 2024 special session, the Legislature approved up to $482 million in incentives for the project, including hundreds of millions in bonding and over $100 million in direct appropriations.

State funds were to go to site preparation, workforce training and infrastructure projects, such as adding an interchange on U.S. Highway 72. In addition, the company also received other local and state tax incentives, such as a 10-year exemption from the state’s corporate income tax.

State economic development leaders say the deal remains on track.

“State incentives associated with the project are performance‑based and time‑bound, and the company’s compliance is evaluated as the project advances. MDA has determined that Amplify Cell remains in compliance with its contractual obligations. Should that status change, the agency will take appropriate action consistent with the agreement,” MDA said in a statement.

It was one of the state’s largest economic development incentives packages according to data from the nonprofit Good Jobs First.

It passed the Legislature in a day with only two senators and one House member voting against it.

“My basic reason for voting ‘no’ was it’s corporate welfare,” said Sen. Kathy Chism, a Republican from New Albany. She contrasts that with what she sees as a lack of incentives and tax breaks for the state’s small businesses.

“I have an issue with state tax dollars going to a Chinese company,” Chism said, referring to EVE Energy, a Chinese company that has 10% ownership in Amplify. In June, the Department of Defense designated EVE as a “Chinese military company.”

A changing market for electric vehicles

Turbulence in the EV market has led to manufacturing delays and cancellations across the U.S.

Since 2022, $18.3 billion of announced EV manufacturing investment has been canceled according to data from Atlas Public Policy, a data and policy research group.

The volatility of the current market is due to a multitude of factors, such as demand lagging behind supply, uneven growth and the expiration of clean vehicle tax credits under the Trump administration.

According to Atlas’ EV Hub, medium- and heavy-duty electric vehicle sales declined significantly year over year, falling from 63,428 vehicles in the first half of 2025 to 43,292 vehicles in the first half of 2026, a decrease of 31.8%.

Some EV battery plants have pivoted to producing batteries to meet the rising demand for power and battery storage from data centers. In June, Amplify did not comment when asked by the Indiana Business Journal whether the factory had been considered for an alternative use.

“Limited construction will continue to ensure that the joint venture remains well positioned for the future while maintaining flexibility,” Daimler said in its first quarter earnings call in May.

text:
Legislation would establish ambitious energy standard to rapidly reduce emissions and achieve up to 100% renewable energy generation by 2046

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Ranking Member of the Senate Agriculture Subcommittee on Rural Development, Energy, and Credit, joined U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and U.S. Representative Yvette Clarke (D-NY-09) in reintroducing the bicameral American Renewable Energy Act (AREA), legislation to establish an ambitious 70% renewable energy resource standard by 2036 to drastically reduce emissions, decrease pollution, and promote community resilience. To achieve this goal, AREA prioritizes the development and implementation of solar, wind, and geothermal energy, as well as marine energy, limited hydropower, and methane digesters for smaller farms and wastewater plants.

The bill also seeks to ensure the equitable distribution of economic, health, and resiliency benefits of renewable energy deployment by establishing an enforcement mechanism that requires at least 50% of collected funds be spent on renewable energy, energy efficiency, and storage projects in impacted communities.

“Taking immediate, ambitious action to reduce emissions and build a clean energy future is essential to combating the climate crisis. Now is the time to enact a national renewable energy standard. Vermont has long led the nation in the clean energy transition, passing historic legislation just this summer that puts us on the path to achieve 100% renewable electricity by 2046,” said Senator Welch. “This bill will help the country follow in Vermont’s footsteps to speed the transition to renewables and build energy independence.”

“As Americans face skyrocketing electricity bills and the increasingly harmful impacts of the climate crisis, unleashing the power of clean energy has never been more important. This legislation will help us accelerate bringing cleaner options for consumers online while reducing emissions, lowering our dependence on fossil fuels and volatile global markets, creating new jobs, and cutting costs for working Americans. This is a key step in our fight towards a cleaner, healthier, and more affordable energy future,” said Senator Van Hollen.

“As we witness the devastating impacts of climate change on communities across our nation, we can no longer afford the luxury of inaction. The choices we make today will determine the world we leave to our children and grandchildren. We have the tools, the technology, and the knowledge to build a cleaner future; we need Congress to act,” said Rep. Clarke. “Investing in renewable energy also means confronting the environmental injustices that have left our nation’s most underserved communities bearing the greatest burden. My legislation puts clean energy technology and innovation to work, reducing emissions, improving air quality and health outcomes, and creating millions of good-paying renewable energy jobs. We cannot leave future generations to pay the price for problems we have the power to solve today.”

AREA would require retail electricity suppliers to achieve at least 20% renewable energy generation in 2027, with an increase to 70% by 2036, and up to 100% by 2046. The bill would also require retail electricity suppliers to strengthen energy resilience by contributing an increasing share of their generation through distributed renewable energy, such as rooftop solar, starting with 15% in 2027, with an increase to 20% deployment requirement after five years.

Additionally, AREA also stipulates that electricity suppliers must meet their requirements by submitting renewable energy credits or paying an alternative compliance payment that begins at $50/megawatts per hour (MWh) and increases with inflation. Compliance with the bill would be facilitated by the creation of six regional credit trading markets to track retail electricity suppliers’ transition to renewable energy and ensure the benefits of renewable energy development are spread across the country.

Further, AREA seeks to ensure the equitable distribution of economic, health, and resiliency benefits and investments created by renewable energy deployment by establishing an enforcement mechanism that requires at least 50% of collected funds to be spent on renewable energy, energy efficiency, and storage projects in impacted communities. The legislation would also require utilities to produce 20% of their energy generation from renewables in impacted communities, reducing the need for polluting fossil fuel power plants in historically marginalized areas.

The American Renewable Energy Act is endorsed by the Chesapeake Climate Action Network; Evergreen Action; Sierra Club; Indivisible; and Vote Solar.

“The American Renewable Energy Act (AREA) is a major step toward building an electric grid that is cleaner, more affordable, and more just. By setting a strong national renewable electricity standard while ensuring that the benefits of the clean energy transition reach frontline and impacted communities, AREA will help reduce harmful pollution, create good-paying jobs, and protect families from the rising costs of fossil fuels. Chesapeake Climate Action Network (CCAN) Action Fund proudly supports AREA and urges Congress to move this bill forward to deliver the clean energy future that American families across the country deserve,” said Quentin Scott, Federal Policy Director, CCAN Action Fund.

“Shifting to renewable energy is no longer just an option, it is the necessary next step for the United States to meet the urgency of the climate crisis. The American Renewable Energy Act is the bold legislation we need to meet rising electricity demand, while improving public health, reducing American reliance on fossil fuels, and creating new jobs to supercharge our clean energy economy,” said Lena Moffitt, Executive Director, Evergreen Action. “The transition to clean energy is well underway and the federal government must be a leader in ensuring Americans benefit from the lower energy costs and cleaner air that renewable energy can deliver.”

“In the last year, electricity cost increases rapidly outpaced the rate of inflation while toxic and deadly emissions from coal plants spiked significantly,” said Patrick Drupp, Climate Policy Director, Sierra Club. “It is more urgent than ever that we invest in affordable, reliable, and clean energy to relieve families from soaring bills and protect our communities from more deadly pollution. Despite Donald Trump’s persistent attacks on clean energy, it is evident that Americans want more clean energy because of how much cleaner, cheaper, and faster it is. We applaud Senator Peter Welch for his work as a steadfast champion of the American Renewable Energy Act and look forward to working together more in the future.”

“A strong federal renewable energy standard establishes a clear national floor for clean energy while preserving states’ ability to pursue even more ambitious policies,” said Nathan Phelps, Managing Director, Vote Solar. “This legislation provides the certainty needed to accelerate investment in affordable, reliable clean energy, expanding access to solar and the benefits of the clean energy transition. By complementing state renewable energy standards, a federal RPS ensures that communities across the country can benefit from lower energy costs, cleaner air, and a stronger economy.”

text:
The debate between panelists at a WisPolitics-State Affairs luncheon on the future of the state Legislature ultimately came down to one question: Is it 2006 or 2010 again?

Former Democratic Senate Majority Leader Chuck Chvala saw a reversal of the red wave that brought a GOP trifecta and handed control of the Legislature to Republicans for the following 16 years.

“I have never seen an election where the problems that people are worried about were driven so directly by one party,” Chvala said during yesterday’s event, rattling off gas prices, the Iran War, tariffs, and healthcare costs. “My gosh, folks, everything that people are upset about is directly because of Donald Trump.”

He was so confident in this assessment that he even predicted the ouster of U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil, R-Janesville, from his 1st CD seat, even though that district hasn’t elected a Democrat since 1992.

For fellow WisOpinion Insider and former GOP Assembly Speaker Scott Jensen, it was 2006, when national discontent over an unpopular president and an unpopular war pushed Republicans out of the Senate but left the GOP with a toehold in the Legislature.

“It’s important to know that voters are frustrated with both parties. If you ask people about both parties, the image of both parties are underwater. People think both parties are worthless,” Jensen said.

But the state Senate, panelists seemed to agree, is destined to go for the Democrats this fall.

Redistricting expert and former GOP lawmaker Joe Handrick noted that all but one of the Senate’s most competitive four seats were open or occupied by a Democrat.

“It’s one thing for an incumbent to swim upstream. It’s entirely different with an open seat and a blue year to swim upstream,” Handrick said.

Debate on the Senate focused on the future of Sen. Howard Marklein, R-Spring Green.

Jensen predicted spending in the matchup between Marklein and Dem Rep. Jenna Jacobson of Oregon could surpass $10 million. WisPolitics tallied a record-setting $11.6 million that was spent in 2024 on Wisconsin’s 8th SD as Dem Jodi Habush Sinykin, of Whitefish Bay, beat then-GOP Sen. Duey Stroebel, of Saukville.

Progressive strategist Victoria Stewart, who once managed a race in Marklein’s district, called him an “incredibly hard worker” and noted his status as a co-chair of the powerful Joint Finance Committee.

“He was everywhere all the time, and we hear this from everyone,” she said, adding, “He also has the opportunity to raise a ton of money, and they are going all in to make sure that they are protecting one of their most powerful members right now.”

Stewart and Chvala also pegged the 25th SD in the state’s northwest corner as an opportunity for a surprise Dem pickup. Bayfield County Supv. Charly Ray faces former Assembly lawmaker Erik Severson.

Panelists were more bearish on Dem chances in the Assembly, which now has a 54-45 GOP majority.

While all four panelists predicted the party would pick up seats, only Chvala predicted an outright majority. Handrick noted incumbent Republicans in that chamber had tended to outrun the top of the ticket going back to 2018.

Jensen cited Assembly Republicans’ immense spending advantage, which Stewart dismissed as coming from a “place of fear,” saying running up campaign spending was “not the only way to win elections.”

Handrick and Jensen both pegged Rep. Ben Franklin, R-De Pere, as the Assembly’s most vulnerable Republican, while Stewart picked a perennial target in Marklein’s district — Rep. Todd Novak of Dodgeville.

On the other hand, Handrick, Jensen and Chvala agreed Rep. Ryan Spaude of Ashwaubenon was the most endangered Democratic incumbent, though Chvala noted the freshman lawmaker had won his first race in a year that Donald Trump had won Wisconsin.

Stewart did not anticipate any Republican pickups in the Assembly but predicted Democrats would pick up only three seats, two shy of a majority.

AUSTIN, Texas, Sept. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- dcbel, the integrated home energy company, today announced the launch of the Ara Core Home Energy Station in Texas, giving homeowners the means to reduce their reliance on an increasingly strained public grid – slashing energy bills while protecting against blackouts from day one.

Through industry-leading intelligent management, Ara Core connects and orchestrates solar panels, home batteries, the public grid, and even bidirectional EVs, creating a private grid that helps homeowners generate, store, and manage their own energy through a groundbreaking all-in-one system. Ara Core's key features include:

100 decisions per second to consume, store, or sell energy with the intelligent Orchestrate OS;

Reduced energy bills with up to 85% independence from the grid;

Blackout protection using solar, battery storage, or a compatible bidirectional EV that can power a home for up to 10 days;

A centralized station that minimizes power losses as it routes energy where needed, providing up to 30% more efficiency over traditional unintegrated energy systems.

To mark its arrival in Texas, dcbel is proud to be powering the 2026 Southern Living Idea House. The custom-built residence in Fredericksburg showcases the latest innovations in architecture, design, and home technology. More than ever, Texans are exploring new energy options such as home batteries, solar panels, and alternative charging solutions to buffer these rising costs and create stability as reliability wavers.

One system for maximum efficiency

The problem? Conventional systems often rely on multiple separate, expensive and complex devices and power conversions that can result in energy losses of up to 30%. In other words, a portion of the energy generated never makes it to where it's needed most.

Ara Core takes a new approach. It's a single point of conversion that intelligently manages home energy with over 100 decisions a second, routing energy between solar panels, home batteries, bidirectional EVs, and the home with minimal losses.

Powered by the Texan sun with Ara Core +solar

It also enables solar to continue powering a home during a blackout.

First in class, built to last

Ara Core is engineered to the highest standards of durability, security, and design.

Built in the USA in collaboration with visionary automotive designer Paul Deutschman, Ara Core features advanced military-grade encryption, stringent UL and CSIP certifications, and a NEMA 3R-rated enclosure suitable for indoor or outdoor installation.

text:
EDF Power Solutions North America has secured funding for a new solar energy project named Utah Solar 1.

Construction can now begin on the 300MW solar farm, which will be located in Utah's Millard County, an area of the US that is extremely popular with renewable energy developers thanks to its sunny climate and vast open plains.

The plant's direct current capacity is rated at 394 MWdc, a figure that reflects the industry practice of installing more panel capacity than the inverters can output at any one moment, since panels rarely all produce at peak levels simultaneously.

EDF hopes that the facility will come online by mid-2027.

"Reaching financial close on Utah Solar 1 reflects strong market confidence in this asset and marks a major milestone for our team," says Amy Lloyd, CFO of EDF Power Solutions North America.

For those unfamiliar with the term 'financial close', this is the point at which a project's funding is contractually locked in and work can begin in earnest.

Who is buying the power?

A 30-year power purchase agreement (PPA) has been signed with the Southern California Public Power Authority (SCPPA), a joint powers agency that procures power on behalf of municipal utilities across the region.

Output will ultimately serve customers of the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP), the largest municipal utility in the US.

EDF estimates that Utah Solar 1 will produce 766,000 megawatt-hours each year, which would be enough to account for a meaningful share of LADWP's clean energy procurement as the utility works towards its own decarbonisation targets.

Long-dated PPAs of this kind remain the financial backbone of utility-scale solar, giving lenders the revenue certainty needed to underwrite construction debt over decades rather than years.

The lenders behind the deal

Capital for the project has come from a total of five banks: Crédit Agricole CIB, MUFG Bank, National Bank of Canada, Societe Generale and Standard Chartered, while MUFG Bank acted as the administrative agent for the facility.

Crédit Agricole CIB, meanwhile, served as initial coordinating lead arranger.

The package also includes a tax credit bridge facility, with Crédit Agricole CIB named as sole buyer of the Production Tax Credits (PTCs) the project will generate.

PTC transfer deals of this sort have become a standard financing tool since the Inflation Reduction Act made such credits transferable, letting developers monetise tax benefits they might otherwise struggle to use directly.

The local impact

Millard County has become something of an American energy hub lately.

text:
Charging networks, battery-swapping stations, fleet depots and supporting power systems emerge as the next phase of the continent’s mobility transition

The vehicle will remain the most visible part of the transition, but the infrastructure around it will determine whether the opportunity delivers”

— Nikhath Zigmund, Senior Advisor to the Africa Transition Acceleration Fund

JOHANNESBURG, SOUTH AFRICA, September 18, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Africa’s electric mobility market is moving from isolated pilots towards commercial adoption, creating investment opportunities that extend beyond vehicles to the infrastructure required to keep them operating.

Sales of electric two-wheelers across Africa reached approximately 70,000 in 2025, more than 80 times the level recorded at the beginning of the decade, according to the International Energy Agency.

According to Nikhath Zigmund, Senior Advisor to the Africa Transition Acceleration Fund, the strongest early demand is emerging among commercial motorcycles, three-wheelers, buses, delivery fleets and logistics vehicles.

“These vehicles travel frequently, follow relatively predictable routes and consume significant amounts of fuel. For their operators, the lifetime cost of a vehicle matters more than its purchase price alone,” says Zigmund.

The economic case is strengthening as battery costs decline. Average global battery prices declined by 8% in 2025, following a 20% reduction in 2024. Electric vehicles can already offer lower running costs in high-use applications because of reduced fuel and maintenance expenses, even where the initial purchase price remains higher.

A motorcycle completing deliveries throughout the day or a bus operating along a fixed route can recover a higher upfront cost more quickly than a vehicle that spends much of its time parked.

The opportunity beyond the vehicle

Electric mobility depends on more than vehicle sales. Charging points, battery-swapping stations, grid connections, fleet depots, maintenance networks, digital payment systems and reliable electricity are all needed for operators to function consistently and expand.

“The vehicle is only one part of the opportunity,” says Zigmund. “Infrastructure serving several manufacturers and fleet operators can offer investors exposure to the wider market without requiring them to predict which individual vehicle brand or technology will eventually dominate.”

Charging networks, battery-swapping stations and electrified fleet depots become more investable when supported by contracted usage, predictable volumes and credible counterparties. These assets also have the potential to generate recurring revenue and be replicated across cities and countries.

Kenya provides an early indication of how mobility demand can translate into infrastructure revenue. Electricity consumed by the country’s e-mobility industry increased by 188% in 2025 to 8.43 GWh.

Kenya’s dedicated e-mobility tariff charges KSh16 per kWh during peak periods and KSh8 during off-peak hours, creating an incentive to charge vehicles when electricity demand is lower.

“Well-managed charging can improve the utilisation of existing power infrastructure and create a growing customer base for utilities,” says Zigmund. “However, grid planning must anticipate the growth of electric fleets to ensure that connections, substations and generation capacity are expanded before constraints emerge.”

Charging facilities can also be combined with renewable generation and battery storage. Solar power located alongside a bus depot, logistics hub or battery-swapping network could reduce pressure on the grid while improving charging reliability.

Different markets, different opportunities

Africa’s electric mobility transition will not follow a single model. South Africa can draw on its established automotive manufacturing base, while Morocco is developing battery and battery-material production, including a gigafactory with an initial planned capacity of 20 GWh.

Markets with substantial motorcycle and informal transport sectors may instead find opportunities in local assembly, battery swapping, fleet leasing and charging networks designed for high-use commercial vehicles.

The financing challenge is moving these businesses from early development to institutional scale. Investment in African electric mobility reached almost USD70 million in 2023, approximately eight times the level recorded in 2021.

“Blended finance and specialised transition capital can support the first depots, charging networks and operating platforms while their business models are refined,” says Zigmund.

“Once utilisation has been demonstrated, contracts established and cash flows made more predictable, these platforms can begin attracting larger pools of institutional capital.”

Electric mobility gives Africa an opportunity to build more than a market for imported vehicles. It can support new electricity demand, stronger utility economics, local industrial capabilities and infrastructure designed around how people and goods move across the continent.

“The vehicle will remain the most visible part of the transition, but the infrastructure around it will determine whether the opportunity delivers,” concludes Zigmund.

KERI said on the 17th that it opened the Capital Charge Yard, a public EV charging interoperability test center, in Sacramento, California, in August and has begun operations.
The facility continuously verifies compatibility between EVs and chargers, based on the interoperability testing framework already running in South Korea.
The project stems from interoperability problems that arise during EV charging.
In 2021, CharIN designated KERI as a global EV interoperability conformity assessment body, and the institute held additional testivals in 2022 and 2024.
text:
CHANGWON — The Korea Electrotechnology Research Institute (KERI) has transplanted to California the electric vehicle charging interoperability testing and verification framework it built in South Korea. As testing technology and operating models developed at home become a benchmark for U.S. public charging infrastructure, Korean EV and charger makers will face a far lighter verification burden when entering the American market.

KERI said on the 17th that it opened the Capital Charge Yard, a public EV charging interoperability test center, in Sacramento, California, in August and has begun operations. The facility continuously verifies compatibility between EVs and chargers, based on the interoperability testing framework already running in South Korea.

The project stems from interoperability problems that arise during EV charging. Charging requires both the coupler, the physical connector, and the charging sequence, the communication protocol through which devices exchange information, to match. Couplers have been largely standardized, but charging sequences have produced errors because manufacturers interpret and apply international standards differently. As next-generation technologies such as Plug and Charge (PnC) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) spread, systems grow more complex and interoperability verification becomes even more important.

KERI has been building the relevant technology since 2018. After Suh Woo-hyun was named team leader of the technology working group at CharIN, the international EV charging consortium, KERI held an EV fast-charging interoperability "testival" that same year with the Korea Smart Grid Association. The format connects vehicles and chargers from multiple companies to one another to identify errors.

In 2021, CharIN designated KERI as a global EV interoperability conformity assessment body, and the institute held additional testivals in 2022 and 2024. Policy experts from the California Energy Commission (CEC) attended the CharIN Conference Asia in 2024 and reviewed KERI's testing and verification framework.

The one-off testival events evolved into a permanent testing facility, later named the Global Interoperability Test Center (GiOTEC). KERI signed agreements in 2024 with Hyundai Motor, Kia, Mercedes-Benz Korea and BMW Korea to establish testing standards, and opened GiOTEC at its Ansan branch in September last year. According to KERI, it is the world's first test center of its kind to conduct continuous cross-verification of EVs and chargers.

Member companies that meet the technical standards can station a vehicle or charger at the center for six months to a year and freely cross-test it against other manufacturers' products. Non-members can apply for short-term testing, and analytical data obtained during testing is shared among participating companies. The structure allows companies to identify and fix charging errors involving products from various manufacturers at home, before shipping products overseas or checking compatibility one by one on site.

The U.S. expansion came after the CEC issued a tender for a permanent verification center to resolve local charging errors. KERI formed a consortium with the U.S. nonprofit Cal EPIC and CharIN, beating out European and other competitors to win the $4 million (about 5.6 billion won) Charge Yard project. KERI said its experience operating GiOTEC and its impartiality as a nonprofit state-funded research institute worked in its favor in the selection. U.S. EV maker Rivian, charging infrastructure company ChargePoint and the Sacramento Municipal Utility District (SMUD) also joined the center as sponsors.

KERI will also use the California center as a venue for international standards verification of next-generation charging technologies. It will serve as technical lead for the CharIN ISO 15118-20 testival to be held there in November, taking the lead on international standards verification for PnC and V2G. The institute plans to build an additional dedicated test center inside the Charge Yard for conformity testing required by the CEC and to carry out initial verification.

"We were able to launch the center quickly through close cooperation with global partners," said Suh Woo-hyun, head of KERI's Intelligent Energy Testing Laboratory. "We will also flawlessly lead the large-scale testival and conformity assessment in November." KERI President Kim Nam-gyun said, "We will build this into a forward base that lets our companies shake off export uncertainty and expand into global markets."

Upon completion of the planned relocation of Line 1 to Thorn Hill, subject to lender approvals, Eos expects the facility to support approximately 4GWh of annual manufacturing capacity across two lines.

The company expects to create jobs across four shifts to staff Line 2 at the Western Pennsylvania facility. Eos stated that the line continues to ramp towards full production as additional shifts come online, consistent with the company’s phased manufacturing scale-up strategy.

Earlier this month, developer-operator MN8 Energy and tech giant Google announced the Mammoth Solar project in Kanawha County, West Virginia, which combines 86MW of solar, 10MW/100MWh of Eos’ Z3 zinc-based long-duration energy storage (LDES) solution, and a 70MW/280MWh lithium-ion (Li-ion) BESS.

In July, Eos received a Golden Dome for America contract from the US Department of Defense (DoD) to integrate mission-ready LDES in support of national defence requirements.

The company will deploy its Z3 solution for the Golden Dome defence initiative announced by President Trump, though the project’s completion within the proposed timeline and its overall delivery remain highly uncertain.

FlexGen and Lightshift expand partnership across 16 BESS projects in Massachusetts, Virginia and Vermont

Software-focused energy storage system integrator FlexGen Power Systems and US storage and solar developer-operator Lightshift Energy are expanding their partnership.

Announced 16 September, the companies are partnering on 16 BESS projects in Massachusetts, Virginia and Vermont, with six projects already operational and ten under construction.

The completed projects deliver more than 25MW/85MWh of storage capacity to the PJM and ISO-NE markets, whilst the projects under construction will add over 55MW/200MWh of capacity.

Lightshift develops, owns and operates the projects, whilst FlexGen provides energy storage software and services, including its FlexGen HybridOS energy management system (EMS).

The partnership began in 2024 with the deployment of FlexGen’s HybridOS EMS at Lightshift’s battery storage project in Groton, Massachusetts. Located adjacent to a local substation, the site provides grid support through peak shaving during high-demand periods.

Since then, Lightshift has selected FlexGen’s HybridOS for additional projects spanning diverse use cases, battery manufacturers and utility customers across New England and the PJM region.

The companies have recently expanded their collaboration by completing a comprehensive integration of FlexGen’s EMS at Lightshift’s BESS facility in Danville, Virginia.

The site provides flexible capacity to Danville Utilities to support peak shaving and demand response programmes during periods of high demand.

The two companies claimed that through a complex upgrade of the battery management system (BMS) and EMS, along with additional battery augmentation, FlexGen and Lightshift enhanced the site’s capacity by 14%, delivering additional grid stability and extending the energy storage asset’s lifespan.

FlexGen and Lightshift plan to continue expanding their portfolio through additional projects, including Danville II, a second 11MW project with Danville Utilities that will function as a peak shaving asset.

HybridOS will serve as the EMS for the ten projects under construction. The software is compatible with more than 80 configurations of batteries and power conversion systems (PCS).

Earlier this month FlexGen and developer SMT Energy announced start of operations of the 160MW/320MWh Houston IV BESS in Houston, Texas.

ESN Premium spoke with Rob Greskowiak, chief commercial officer at Lightshift, about the company’s distributed storage approach to meeting rising electricity demand in PJM, including the massive impact of data centre developments, in April.

The company announced on 16 April a five-project, distribution-scale battery storage portfolio across Virginia.

Greskowiak noted in that interview, “The thesis has always been ‘bigger is better.’ If I’m going to go build a project and mobilise a construction crew and get an interconnect position, I’d much rather build 500MW than 50MW for economies of scale purposes. While I think that’s true for a lot of generating resources, I think battery storage specifically as an asset class has bucked that trend.”

Georgia Power brings 128MW Robins battery facility into commercial operation

Utility Georgia Power has brought its 128MW Robins Battery Facility into commercial operation near Warner Robins, Georgia.

Announced 15 September, the facility can deliver stored energy to the grid for up to four hours (512MWh) and is paired with the nearby Robins Solar Facility.

State and local officials, alongside leaders from Robins Air Force Base, attended a ceremony to mark the commercial operation of the project. Attendees included Robins Air Force Base Col. Johari Hemphill, Senator Larry Walker, Senator David Lucas, Senator Steven McNeel, Representative Anissa Jones, Central Georgia Joint Development Authority Chairman James Vaughn, and Macon-Bibb County Mayor Lester Miller.

Burns & McDonnell served as the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractor for the Robins Battery Facility and delivered the project on schedule.

The Robins BESS is one of four BESS projects approved in the 2023 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) update by the Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC). Georgia Power has completed battery storage facilities in Cherokee and Lowndes counties totalling 579.5MW and is nearing completion of a 57.5MW facility in Floyd County.

The PSC has also approved nine additional BESS facilities across eight sites statewide, adding more than 3,000MW of energy storage capacity. Sites were selected based on their ability to efficiently support grid operations, including proximity to existing infrastructure, substations and company-owned properties.

Planned facilities include locations at Plants Bowen, Hammond, McIntosh, Wansley and Yates, as well as stand-alone sites in Hall and McDuffie counties.

Georgia Power has also received approval for two solar facilities paired with battery storage, providing a combined 350MW of generating capacity. The new solar-plus-storage facilities will be located in Laurens and Mitchell counties.

The project is part of Georgia Power’s broader strategy to add cost-effective energy resources through the PSC’s IRP process.

title: Senate bill on carbon dioxide wells threatens rural water supplies - The Hill
authors: Ted Schettler and Liz Barbour, opinion contributors, Ted Schettler, Liz Barbour, opinion contributors
description:
The U.S. Senate is considering legislation that will weaken groundwater protections, pertaining to wells engineered for long-term storage of carbon dioxide.
This section would direct EPA “to provide for exemptions that allow the use of non-potable aquifers for Class VI wells.” There are two exemptions in the bill.
The carbon dioxide was to be primarily sourced from Wyoming gas plants and sequestered via up to 15 wells.
However, projects like this one have a greater chance of moving forward if the law is changed to permit these carbon dioxide wells to be sited near aquifers used for rural wells and watering livestock.
This bill, exempting aquifers not currently used for drinking water (by people), imperils the livelihoods of small rural communities dependent on ranching and farming.
text:
The U.S. Senate is considering legislation that will weaken groundwater protections, pertaining to wells engineered for long-term storage of carbon dioxide.

The language in question is buried in the last section of a larger water resources package, titled “Non-potable Aquifer Exemption for Class VI Wells” from the Water Resources Development Act of 2026. This section would direct EPA “to provide for exemptions that allow the use of non-potable aquifers for Class VI wells.”

There are two exemptions in the bill. One applies if “the aquifer, or portion of the aquifer, does not currently serve as a source of drinking water” and “cannot now and will not in the future serve as a source of drinking water.” The other applies if “the total dissolved solids content of the ground water from the aquifer, or portion of the aquifer,” is between 3 and 10 grams per liter, and “the aquifer, or portion of the aquifer, is not reasonably expected to supply a public water system.”

That may sound complex, but here’s the reality: These two exemptions would discriminate against small rural communities and especially harm rural ranchers and farmers, because they could exempt irrigation water and water used for livestock watering operations. The problem is that just because people aren’t drinking or aren’t expected to drink the water, it follows that its content is irrelevant.

In addition, the exemptions would allow these carbon dioxide wells to be situated beneath or near aquifers that, while not being used currently for drinking water by people, could be in the future given the availability of reverse osmosis and other emerging water treatment technologies.

If a Class VI well were to leak carbon dioxide into an aquifer used for irrigation and livestock, it would acidify the water and mobilize heavy metals and potentially other toxic materials rendering it unusable in agriculture or for any drinking water purposes now or in the future.

Well documented well failures at injection wells in Illinois and Texas have shown that carbon capture injection wells need more stringent protections, not less.

This legislation would have had a direct impact on a proposed project in Montana, exempting certain aquifers from review when EPA considers Class VI well permits. The Snowy River Carbon Sequestration Project was a proposed ExxonMobil (via Denbury Carbon Solutions) facility in southeastern Montana’s Carter County designed to inject 150 million tons of carbon dioxide underground over 20 years. The carbon dioxide was to be primarily sourced from Wyoming gas plants and sequestered via up to 15 wells.

Landowners, including farmers and ranchers, were opposed because they saw no meaningful economic benefit but rather threats to range land and livelihoods, including degradation of surface and groundwater resources. The EPA found the Bureau of Land Management environmental assessment of potential impacts on groundwater aquifers inadequate. These included several shallow alluvial plain aquifers and a deeper sandstone aquifer. The shallower aquifers were primarily used for watering livestock, although they did qualify as underground sources of drinking water.

Facing heavy local and environmental scrutiny over agricultural disruption, groundwater threats, and pipeline safety, the bureau scaled back its review. Instead of approving the entire project footprint, the agency authorized only a single stratigraphic test well on state land to collect geologic and hydrologic data. Recently, Exxon removed the permit application, in large part due to the massive local opposition. However, projects like this one have a greater chance of moving forward if the law is changed to permit these carbon dioxide wells to be sited near aquifers used for rural wells and watering livestock.

This bill, exempting aquifers not currently used for drinking water (by people), imperils the livelihoods of small rural communities dependent on ranching and farming. It should be stopped.

text:
Rooftops are great places for solar panels. Widespread adoption of solar and storage on homes improves the resiliency of the electrical grid, can protect homeowners from blackouts, reduce health-harming pollution from electricity production, and provide financial savings for families.

But there’s a problem. Today, millions of roofs that could host solar panels are not being put to use for that purpose, and research suggests that bureaucratic red tape is a big reason why. On a webinar hosted by Environment America, advocates joined permitting officials and solar company leaders to share research and ideas for how state leaders can streamline permitting, inspection and interconnection of residential rooftop solar systems to help more people power their lives with solar energy. Click on the link to watch a recording of the webinar.

Kirby suggested that if rules for the solar market could be simplified and standardized, it could drive down costs and support more clean energy adoption. If the U.S. succeeded in driving down costs so that solar cost $1.00 per watt, 18 million more American families could get solar, according to Permit Power research.

The next speaker on the panel was Renee Merieaux, who has worked for 30 years processing permits for city building departments in California and Colorado. Merieaux shared how city offices process solar permits and showed how automated computer software can approve permits instantly while keeping homes safe. She explained that, in her experience, instant permitting software saves city workers a lot of time because permits get checked by the software right away. Merieaux explained that state laws are needed to make local offices switch to instant permitting processes.

Nicholas Manto, the founder & CEO of The Solar Scouts, installs solar panels in Texas. He explained how a new law in Texas requires jurisdictions to review and approve a solar project or request revisions within two days, at which point third-parties are allowed to conduct the permitting and inspection. In the case of third party review, automated permitting software or a professional engineer or a master electrician reviews the plans and signs off on the permits, and can then follow up with an inspection. Manto said many jurisdictions are following through with that and that in those places, The Solar Scouts is seeing a much faster review timeline.

Solutions to help rooftop solar grow

To cut permitting-related red tape and bring clean solar energy to more homes, states can implement a number of steps, which are outlined in the Environment Massachusetts Research & Policy Center’s Solar Permitting Scorecard.

They include:

automating solar permitting by requiring jurisdictions to adopt automated permitting to eliminate needless delays.

Improving the inspection process by restricting the number of required inspections and allowing for remote and virtual inspections.

Standardizing regulations and fees and reducing variability across jurisdictions.

Kirby also referenced the importance of streamlining the processes around connecting a home solar system with the electric grid. He suggested that reforms could include improved transparency in the utility interconnection process, moving to automated interconnection, which would be the gold standard, and ensuring fair cost allocation across all users in the electric system that benefit from the widespread adoption of residential rooftop solar.

Take action

To make the most of rooftop solar, states need to replace their traditional process with instant permitting – and more. Take action today and urge your state lawmakers to cut red tape to expand rooftop solar in your state.

text:
On September 14, Lee Zeldin, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, signed the final order repealing the majority of the Biden administration’s greenhouse gas (GHG) requirements for U.S. power plants.

Zeldin made the announcement at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston, Texas, and he said the action will save $310 billion. He also proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse gas standard for the power sector.

Zeldin had announced EPA’s intention to repeal all greenhouse gas emissions standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants on June 11, when he wrote, “The EPA is proposing that the Clean Air Act (CAA) requires it to make a finding that GHG emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants contribute significantly to dangerous air pollution, as a predicate to regulating GHG emissions from those plants.”

Barge Effects

The repeal could directly affect the demand for open hopper barges because it could halt or slow the enforced decline of coal cargoes on the rivers. Even with the years-long decline in coal cargoes due to regulatory pressure on coal-fired power plants, coal still makes up about 25 percent of all barge cargoes, according to the Corps of Engineers’ Center for Waterborne Statistics. In the longer term, the effect would likely be a slowing or stabilizing, perhaps with a slight uptick, rather than a reversal of longer-term trends eroding coal cargoes.

Endangerment Finding

Zeldin’s action is part of the Trump administration’s plan to completely reverse, in practical and regulatory terms, the Supreme Court’s finding in Massachusetts v. EPA that greenhouse gases are “air pollution.” The ruling marked a milestone in both climate law and in EPA’s regulatory powers. Before that ruling, the term “air pollution” referred only to substances directly harmful to human health, like mercury, particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide or sulfur dioxide.

Zeldin’s EPA repealed the endangerment finding in February — the finding required by Massachusetts v. EPA that if EPA wanted to regulate greenhouse gases, it had to find them “dangerous to human health,” which that era’s EPA did in 2009. At the time, Chris Field, director of the Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment, said of the endangerment finding, “It’s the foundation on which all of the other regulations rest. It is the authorization to regulate greenhouse gasses, and, without that authorization, the legal basis for regulating emissions from automobiles and power plants is fuzzy at best and potentially non-existent.”

In March, Zeldin said, “We are driving a dagger straight into the heart of the climate change religion to drive down cost of living for American families, unleash American energy, bring auto jobs back to the U.S. and more.”

In pursuing this strategy, the EPA relied on narrow legal arguments and definitions rather than broader fights over science. “Whether CAA section 202(a)(1) authorizes the EPA to regulate in response to global climate change concerns by prescribing emission standards is a matter of statutory interpretation, not scientific analysis,” the EPA said.

However, even the libertarian Cato Institute, which agrees in substance with not including greenhouse gases as “air pollutants,” argued that the EPA’s attempt to circumvent Massachusetts v. EPA is unconvincing.

In other words, extended court fights are sure to follow.
