text:
This week’s Infrastructure & Incentives Update from Business Facilities for site selection decision-makers features the latest from Indiana, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, and a survey on airports from around the U.S. and Canada.

Power Up Indiana Boosts Healthcare Careers

Through the Power Up Indiana program, residents have increased access to build careers in healthcare while giving employers the skilled workforce they need to grow. Power Up Indiana invests in employer-led training that expands opportunity for workers and addresses workforce shortages across the health care sector.

Administered by the Indiana Department of Workforce Development, Power Up Indiana supports Governor Mike Braun’s strategy to help employers grow by developing talent from within, creating new career pathways and growing wages for Hoosiers while addressing workforce needs in key industries.

At Deaconess Health System, the Power Up investment is helping existing employees advance into high-demand clinical careers through the expansion of Step Up, a program that allows frontline employees to earn professional credentials while continuing to receive their regular wages. More than 100 employees are enrolled in pathways including nursing, sonography, medical imaging, laboratory technology, medical assisting and medical coding.

DaMar Staffing Solutions is expanding Indiana’s community-based healthcare workforce by preparing professionals who help patients navigate care and address barriers such as transportation and housing. With support from Power Up, DaMar focuses on upskilling community health workers, registered nurse coordinators, caregiver guides, transition specialists and patient service representatives.

$125M For Life Sciences Innovation In Pennsylvania

At a ribbon-cutting this week for Madrigal Pharmaceuticals’ headquarters in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania, the Pennsylvania Department of Community and Economic Development (DCED) Secretary Rick Siger highlighted the recently created Innovate in PA 2.0 program.

The program builds on previous investments in life sciences by closing key gaps between invention and commercialization. And for the first time, Innovate in PA 2.0 introduces programs tailored to the life sciences industry to expand career pathways, simplify and speed up clinical trials, and increase venture capital opportunities.

“Madrigal is doing lifesaving research and development right here in Pennsylvania, and I’m honored to help celebrate the opening of their new headquarters in Conshohocken,” said Secretary Siger.

“Governor Shapiro secured up to $125 million for the new Innovate in PA 2.0 program to cultivate an environment where more innovators like Madrigal can thrive. Our Commonwealth is home to some of the brightest innovators and researchers in the country, and Madrigal is an excellent example of the kind of innovation and growth the Shapiro Administration is fostering across Pennsylvania.”

Tennessee Launches QUBIT Grant Program

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee and Deputy Gov. and Department of Economic and Community Development Commissioner Stuart C. McWhorter announced the launch of the Tennessee Quantum Utilization Buildout Infrastructure and Technology (QUBIT) Grant Program, housed under TNECD’s Office of Innovation.

The program allocates $43 million to support the physical and digital shared-use infrastructure and support network needed to connect Tennessee’s quantum assets and expand access to quantum technologies statewide. Applications will be accepted through October 23, 2026.

The projects selected will aim to strengthen regional quantum hubs, expand quantum cloud access, establish open-access testbeds and advance a coordinated statewide quantum infrastructure network.

Eligible projects may include:

Regional quantum network expansion

Open-access quantum networking testbeds

Statewide quantum cloud access

Institutional and regional access nodes

Quantum sensing and secure communications infrastructure

Cybersecurity and interoperability infrastructure

Supporting infrastructure

“Between Oak Ridge National Laboratory, EPB’s vast quantum network, leading research universities and an ever-growing technology sector, Tennessee has the foundation to become a national hub for quantum innovation,” said Deputy Gov. and Commissioner McWhorter.

The QUBIT Grant Program is open to the following Tennessee-based eligible applicants: public or private nonprofit higher education institutions, development districts, Oak Ridge National Laboratory or public utilities. These applicants may lead consortia of project partners including for-profit companies, national or regional laboratories, nonprofit organizations, utilities, educational institutions, economic development organizations and other public or private entities.

Click here to view program guidelines, application materials and submission instructions.

JD Power Surveys Airport Satisfaction In U.S., Canada

Released September 16, the JD Power 2026 North America Airport Satisfaction Study suggests the nation’s airports are finding ways to defy the odds. Thanks in large part to dozens of major airport capital improvement projects finally reaching completion, overall passenger satisfaction with airports in North America increases significantly in 2026, despite passenger volume continuing to run at or near the record levels set in 20251.

“For the better part of the last decade, nearly every airport, from the largest international hubs to midsized airfields, has undertaken a significant capital improvement project aimed at streamlining passenger flow, adding attractive food and beverage options and improving overall passenger experience,” said Michael Taylor, managing director of travel, hospitality and retail at JD Power. “On the whole, those efforts are finally starting to pay off in the form of higher overall passenger satisfaction scores. However, when it comes to the individual experiences of passengers, every detail counts and the specific design and structural decisions airports make can have a significant influence on how passengers spend their time – and their money – in the terminal.”

The JD Power 2026 North America Airport Satisfaction Study measures overall passenger satisfaction with mega, large and medium North American airports by examining their experience across seven core dimensions (in order of importance): ease of travel through airport; level of trust with airport; terminal facilities; airport staff; departure/to airport experience; food, beverage and retail; and arrival/from airport experience.

Mega airports are defined as those with 33 million or more passengers per year; large airports with 10 to 32.9 million passengers per year; and medium airports with 4.5 to 9.9 million passengers per year.

Mega Airports: Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport ranks highest in passenger satisfaction among mega airports for a third consecutive year, with a score of 684. Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (663) ranks second and Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (642) ranks third.

Large Airports: Tampa International Airport ranks highest among large airports with a score of 715. Portland International Airport (Oregon) (708) ranks second and Dallas Love Field (698) ranks third.

Medium Airports: Charleston International Airport ranks highest among medium airports with a score of 712. Ontario International Airport (California) (705) ranks second and Indianapolis International Airport (695) ranks third.

The 2026 study is based on 24,710 completed surveys from U.S. or Canadian residents who traveled through at least one U.S. or Canadian airport and covers both departure and arrival experiences (including connecting airports) during the past 30 days. Passengers evaluated either a departing or arriving airport from their round-trip experience. The study was fielded from July 2025 through July 2026.

text:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's latest directive signals increased regulatory pressure on data center development in the Lone Star State. On September 14, 2026, Gov. Abbott directed the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) to "use its statutory authority to compel major water users to comply with water use reporting requirements and to impose legal consequences for past and future failure to comply with state law."

In the September 14 letter to the agency's chairwoman and its executive administrator, Abbott stated the agency's statutory duty to develop statewide water planning and that large-volume water users are legally obligated to respond to the TWDB survey with "complete and accurate information." Abbott then explicitly stated that failure by large water users such as data centers to provide complete responses may result in legal consequences, including civil penalties, ineligibility to obtain permits and even criminal charges.

Abbott further directed the TWDB to coordinate with the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) on its ongoing audit of data centers. The audit is expected to include a study of proposed projects' water use and efficiency, although ERCOT's regulatory purview has historically been limited to electrical power. Finally, Abbott restated his August 3, 2026, directive that failure by a large-volume water user to respond to the TWDB survey should result in denial of interconnection to the ERCOT grid.

As Holland & Knight has previously reported, Abbott's response comes as the dramatic increase in data center development in rural Texas impacts nearby residents, an important constituency in a midterm election cycle. The Texas Legislature has largely followed the governor's lead, with a number of Texas House and Senate committees studying the issue and signaling major changes ahead in the coming legislative session in January 2027.

text:
La Plata Electric Association has been moving full force into a new era of energy independence since exiting its contract with Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association earlier this year.

“We are now moving beyond the transition, and we’re getting elbows deep into the really hard decisions of what does the future of La Plata Electric look like,” Nicole Pitcher, LPEA board president, said at a community open house Monday.

The open house was intended to give residents a look at what that future is shaping up to be – a diverse energy portfolio.

LPEA is pursuing a host of new projects and power procurement contracts, all centered on two key priorities: keeping energy rates stable for members and reducing carbon emissions.

LPEA is working to develop projects and energy contracts that include a mix of resources, including wind, solar, battery storage, gas-fired generation and hydropower, LPEA CEO Chris Hansen said in an interview with The Durango Herald.

“If you think of that idea as a symphony, we’re trying to be the conductor and get all these different types of power sources acting in concert and complementing each other,” he said.

LPEA has reduced its carbon emissions by about 62% and is targeting an 82% reduction by 2030, Hansen told those attending Monday’s open house.

Several additional projects and updates within the county are in the works, namely the expansion of Sunnyside Solar and the implementation of battery energy storage systems.

Other contracts for energy suppliers located throughout the state, including a wind power contract, are also planned.

The co-op is actively pursuing a 50- to 75-megawatt “right-sized” wind project, which likely would be located on the Eastern Plains of Colorado or another high-quality wind area outside La Plata County, Hansen said. The project would be developed in partnership with other small utilities.

While LPEA intends to continue emphasizing and diversifying its renewable energy sources, nonrenewable resources remain part of the co-op’s plans.

LPEA is currently negotiating a power purchase agreement that would include gas-fired generation within or near its service territory, Hansen said.

“Gas-fired generation and wind power are great complements to each other. They don’t compete directly,” he said. “We’re just really trying to get the best of both types of technology.”

Further into the future, LPEA could add geothermal energy to its portfolio as research and development into the technology continues in Colorado and across the West, Hansen said.

That option, however, would not be considered until the early to mid-2030s, he said.

La Plata County solar expansion

The Sunnyside Solar farm expansion has been submitted to the county planning department and is awaiting comment, Hansen said.

The plans propose the expansion of the farm’s generating capacity from 1.7 MW to 5.0 MW. It also includes the BESS facility, which would add 5 MW of storage and be located at the Sunnyside Substation just outside Durango city limits.

A first try at industrial scale battery energy storage systems at a substation in the county is in planning following the approval of county BESS land-use codes. The hope is to shift mid‑day surplus solar into evening peaks which would reduce the expense of peak-hour power and strengthen the reliability of renewable energy sources.

The approval of BESS by county commissioners early in the year was controversial, as some residents in the area of the planned location argued that the technology will be disrupting and, more over, pose a serious safety risk.

Older BESS technology has led to several catatrosphic fires in the past few years, however LPEA has repeatedly said that the batteries it plans to use – Tesla Megapack 2XL lithium batteries, according to planning documents – do not have the same risky chemical composition as the ones involved in the fires.

Because it would be the co-op’s first deployment of such technology, Hansen said the project will begin small and be developed in incremental stages so as to gain operational experience. Additionally, he said that it allows LPEA to be able to adopt new, updated battery technology as they are developed.

The county’s decision is expected later this year and construction could begin immediately after approval, Hansen said.

According to planning documents, the project would be up and running midway through 2028.

As planned, it would provide roughly 4% to 5% of peak demand on a hot summer day at full output and over a full year would contribute roughly 2% to 3% of the full power supply, according to planning documents.

The BESS facility would employ six Tesla Megapack 2XL lithium batteries and inverters, along with a variety of transformers to store and release electricity.

Wholesale energy costs going down

Even with many more projects and contracts in the works, wholesale energy has dropped in just several months since the Tri-State exit.

Since then, LPEA’s wholesale power costs are roughly 12% lower than they would have been under Tri-State, based on real numbers, Hansen said.

The financial impact is “crystal clear,” he said. That reduction however, does not mean that members are experiencing price cuts as delivery costs rise sharply.

Materials like steel, aluminum, copper, transformers and wires have experienced nearly a 10% inflation costs largely driven by high tariffs on metal goods, Hansen said.

“Those costs are hitting everybody in the utility industry across the board,” he said.

LPEA is involved in state and federal level advocacy, but Hasen said the Federal Administration has been unresponsive.

Regardless of tariffs, LPEA does not foresee rates going down as electricity demand rises nationally.

“There’s really not a pathway for electricity prices to decrease. What we’re trying to do is hold them as steady as we can,” Hansen said.

text:
The startup Mazama Energy just nabbed $135 million to accelerate its next-generation geothermal activities near Oregon’s Newberry Volcano.

Mazama is seeking to generate clean electricity from superhot rocks — an emerging and largely unproven approach that could have an enormous payoff for the power sector. That’s because the hotter the geothermal resource, the fewer expensive wells companies have to drill to build powerful and efficient systems.

“Superhot rock is almost essential for geothermal to become cost-competitive with fossil fuels,” Sriram Vasantharajan, Mazama’s CEO, told Canary Media ahead of Thursday’s announcement.

The Frisco, Texas–based company said its new funding includes an oversubscribed Series B led by the billionaire John Arnold’s Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital. Oil and gas giants ConocoPhillips and Shell Ventures also participated, as did existing investors Khosla Ventures and Gates Frontier.

“Superhot geothermal offers the promise of firm, carbon-free power with a relatively small footprint, but realizing that promise requires significant technical innovation,” Arnold said in a news release. ​“Mazama has made impressive progress, and I am excited to support its next phase of development.”

Mazama’s announcement follows a flurry of activity within the next-gen geothermal sector. The startup Fervo Energy went public earlier this year, then its Utah project landed a huge power-purchase deal with Google. Sage Geosystems recently started producing power from its first pilot system in Texas. And Quaise Energy — which is also drilling a geothermal well near Newberry Volcano — closed a $180 million funding round last month.

All these geothermal companies are trying to break the constraints that have held back traditional projects in the U.S. and globally.

Conventional plants rely on natural pockets of hot water to heat fluids and drive turbines. Newer firms and old-school geothermal giants alike are developing technologies to harness heat from hot, dry rocks that could potentially unlock hundreds of gigawatts of around-the-clock power in the western U.S. Enhanced geothermal systems in particular involve drilling several miles into the earth and fracturing rocks to create artificial reservoirs.

Mazama, like many of its competitors, has its roots in the fossil fuel industry.

Vasantharajan is a chemical engineer who previously worked on complex oil and gas wells, including in deep-water and heavy petroleum reservoirs. In 2023, Mazama launched with the goal of developing innovative drilling tools and techniques to extract heat from harsh, superhot environments.

The startup hit its first major milestone last October: Mazama said it built the world’s hottest enhanced geothermal system — reaching 331 degrees Celsius (629 degrees Fahrenheit) — at its pilot site near the Newberry Volcano. The project, which received a U.S. Department of Energy grant, earned praise at the time from industry experts.

“This proof of concept opens the door to deeper and hotter opportunities at Newberry and beyond,” said John McLennan of Utah Forge, a federally funded geothermal laboratory in Beaver County, Utah.

Mazama reached a depth of 10,350 feet for its first well. For its second, the company hit the same depth about 80% faster this year — a key improvement when rigs can cost over $100,000 per day to operate. Mazama continues to drill down thousands more feet as it seeks to hit 400℃, a temperature at which such a project could deliver up to 10 times more power than a conventional 200℃ well, according to Mazama.

The new financing will fund Mazama’s next initiative: Project Ceres, which is supported by the Department of Energy. It involves drilling horizontally to demonstrate the potential for 15 megawatts of clean electricity capacity from each well. Vasantharajan said the startup plans to start drilling wells later this year and start testing the system early next year.

“Ceres becomes our blueprint for our scalable, commercial pathway for deployment of superhot rock,” he said.

text:
Abstract

As Indiana transitions toward electric mobility, data-driven planning is essential to guide electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure investment and deployment. This study evaluates the current and future performance of Indiana’s EV charging infrastructure using Multimodal Energy-Efficient Trip Simulation in Real Time (METS-R), a high-resolution simulation platform. Five EV adoption scenarios, ranging from pessimistic to optimistic, are modeled for the years 2024 through 2031, to assess spatial and temporal variations in public charging demand. Results reveal increasing public charging demand under high adoption scenarios, with significant disparities between urban and non-urban areas. Accessibility to public charging is found to be uneven across Indiana, with access to Direct Current Fast Charging (DCFC) more limited than to Level 2 (L2) chargers. Demand-to-supply analysis identifies Zip Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs) with high EV demand relative to accessible charging supply, highlighting priority areas for targeted deployment. Temporal variations in charging demand underscore the importance of time-of-day planning, while vehicle miles traveled (VMT) analysis highlights the dominant role of local roads usage in EV travel. Revenue projections indicate substantial market potential but also underscore the importance of strategic siting and accurate forecasting, with a median return on investment (ROI) of approximately 0.90 over an 8-year period. The estimated economic development impacts include approximately 2,000 jobs, $130 million in earnings, and $400 million in gross output. The study concludes with actionable recommendations for the Indiana Department of Transportation (INDOT) and stakeholders to guide EV infrastructure investment and deployment, including scenario-based planning, accessibility-informed location prioritization, and targeted deployment in areas with high demand-to-supply ratio.

text:
Despite more than four hours of discussion on the conservation requirements for the long-embattled New England Clean Energy Connect project, the state environmental board held off on making a final ruling on the issue.

Instead, the Board of Environmental Protection on Thursday directed department staff to review its proposed order and add additional analysis before it is revisited.

Last year, the Maine Department of Environmental Protection approved the project’s conservation plan as part of the construction of 53 miles of new transmission line through western Maine. The $1.65 million interconnection project owned by Central Maine Power parent company Iberdrola carries hydroelectric power from Quebec to several New England states.

The citizen-led Board of Environmental Protection, an independent body that oversees the enforcement of environmental laws, met to consider an appeal of the department’s decision, filed by the Appalachian Mountain Club, Maine Audubon, Natural Resources Council of Maine and Trout Unlimited.

David Kallin, who represents the groups, said the conservation plan “categorically fails” to meet the standards set by the board, calling it a “shell game on multiple levels.”

The groups argue that the conservation area set aside by NECEC doesn’t meet the board’s earlier standards, and instead should be less fragmented, with more old-growth forest.

“The board must recognize that this is a bad plan that does not meet the words, let alone the intent, of the habitat fragmentation mitigation that you’ve already ordered,” Kallin said.

But Lisa Gilbreath, attorney for NECEC LLC, said the conservation groups were the ones that demanded the area be protected.

“The record is stuffed with testimony and filings by appellants that directly contradict this appeal,” she said. “To put it in polite terms, it really doesn’t pass the straight face test.”

Kallin argued that the area in NECEC’s easement is mostly made up of juvenile forest and will need several decades of growth to be considered mature — while the damage done by the corridor has already happened.

“There are lots of options that could have been brought forward, where actual mature forest exists on the ground today, not a half century from today, and where those could have been protected in some meaningful way,” Kallin said.

But Gilbreath countered that the easement was deliberately selected as a high conservation value area, and the groups have not identified another section of land that would be a better option.

“By their definition, it needs to be entirely unfragmented, can’t be near Route 201, it can’t be near any other fragmenting feature,” she said. “They haven’t pointed to one piece of property that would satisfy it.”

She argued that the land does have sufficient mature forest, and the groups were “making demands that simply are not required,” adding that NECEC selected the conservation easement as close to the corridor as possible because conservation groups, and then the board, required that it be near the area impacted by the project.

Kallin also pointed to comments submitted by several state agencies that specified that the definition of a mature forest in the conservation plan should not be considered precedent for future projects.

“Throughout all of this time, (NECEC) has claimed that the state agencies were holding them to task to compensate for the fragmentation impacts of this project, but Maine’s natural resource agencies are waving a warning flag for you,” Kallin said. “There’s no getting around the fact that any decision made on this project will be a precedent.”

Gilbreath said that will not be the case.

“There’s no precedent here,” she said. “The department knows, the board knows, every single project is treated differently. Every single order is different based on specifics of that project.”

description:
The rising e-waste volume represents a potential US$3.5 billion black mass recovery market opportunity.
Black mass recycling separates and refines these components to recover valuable metals for reuse in the production of new batteries.
India’s Black Mass Recycling Capacity India has the capacity to recycle over 60,000 tonnes of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) annually, which could yield approximately 30,000 tonnes of black mass.
Black mass recycling can help reduce India’s import dependence, but its contribution depends on whether recovered minerals re-enter domestic battery production.
Black mass recycling can help reduce India’s import dependence, but its contribution depends on whether recovered minerals re-enter domestic battery production.
text:
Image Source: Getty Images

Demand for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) in India is driven by the automotive industry for electric vehicles (EVs). With EV sales reaching 2.3 million units in 2025 and a target of 30 percent of all vehicle sales being electric by 2030, India’s LIB demand is projected to increase from 15 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in 2025 to 127 GWh by 2030. This creates a dual challenge: securing battery raw materials such as lithium and nickel, which are currently 100 percent imported, and managing the resulting e-waste, expected to reach 14 million tonnes by 2030.

The rising e-waste volume represents a potential US$3.5 billion black mass recovery market opportunity. Black mass is a powder-like substance obtained from shredding discarded LIBs and consumer electronics. It contains anode and cathode materials, including critical minerals such as lithium, nickel and graphite, as well as residual electrolytes. Black mass recycling separates and refines these components to recover valuable metals for reuse in the production of new batteries.

India’s policy framework must complement black mass recycling incentives with measures that connect recyclers with domestic battery-material and cell manufacturers — creating reliable offtake for recovered materials and supporting the development of a domestic battery supply chain.

For recycling to reduce import dependence and contribute to a circular domestic battery supply chain, the recovered material needs off-takers that can refine it into battery-grade minerals and process it further into precursors, cathode active materials (CAMs), and anode active materials (AAMs). These battery materials must then feed into cell manufacturing and, subsequently, battery packs for deployment in sectors such as EVs, energy storage systems and electronics.

Figure 1: Lithium-ion Battery Supply Chain

Source: Authors’ own, based on data from ORF America

India’s policy framework must complement black mass recycling incentives with measures that connect recyclers with domestic battery-material and cell manufacturers — creating reliable offtake for recovered materials and supporting the development of a domestic battery supply chain.

India’s Black Mass Recycling Capacity

India has the capacity to recycle over 60,000 tonnes of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) annually, which could yield approximately 30,000 tonnes of black mass. This recycling and refining is carried out primarily through two methods: hydrometallurgy, a water-based process for extracting metals, and pyrometallurgy, a heat-based extraction and purification process.

Critical minerals recovered from black mass vary depending on the battery chemistry. While the anodes (graphite coated with copper), electrolyte (lithium salt) and separator are similar across chemistries, the cathode composition differs. The two most widely used cathode chemistries are lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC).

India mostly uses LFP batteries, which are over 40 percent cheaper than NMC alternatives and account for over half of EV batteries globally. Therefore, black mass in India may have varying proportions of lithium, iron, copper and graphite.

Since the capacity to process black mass is limited, it is usually exported to foreign refineries without extracting the critical minerals embedded within it. Domestic recyclers supplement locally available feedstock with imports from overseas markets including Europe, the Middle East, Australia and Japan. These include Attero, with a recycling capacity of approximately 15,000 tonnes per annum, and Lohum, which holds over 90 percent of India’s integrated LIB recycling market.

Figure 2: Non-Exhaustive List of Stakeholders in India’s LIB Recycling Sector

Source: RMI

To encourage domestic recycling, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change classifies black mass as “hazardous waste” due to its combustible and toxic properties. Consequently, the import and export of black mass require written permission from the Ministry under the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016.

Restricting exports without simultaneously developing domestic processing capacity poses a challenge.

Restricting exports without simultaneously developing domestic processing capacity poses a challenge. The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs has reported instances of LIB shredding units exporting hazardous black mass under incorrect trade codes, highlighting that the domestic refining ecosystem has not yet scaled sufficiently to absorb the black mass produced.

Policy landscape

1. Battery Recycling and Processing

India’s policy framework has begun to recognise spent LIBs as a valuable resource rather than merely a waste stream. Spent LIBs typically have a service life of 5–8 years and, once recycled, could supply more than 40 percent of the country’s lithium demand.

The Battery Waste Management (BWM) Rules, 2022 mandate the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) to develop a centralised online portal for waste management. In January 2025, the CPCB issued a standard operating procedure for the utilisation of black mass generated from dismantling and recycling of LIBs. Under these rules, battery producers and importers are subject to Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) obligations, which prohibit the disposal of batteries in landfills and require them to undertake or authorise other entities to collect, recycle or refurbish a proportion of waste batteries according to battery type and application.

The CPCB also released the Guidelines for Recycling of Waste Batteries in July 2026 for managing waste lead-acid and lithium-ion batteries. They provide detailed requirements for recycling facilities, including infrastructure for LIB shredding facilities and emissions standards in the work zone.

Regulatory measures are being complemented by fiscal incentives. In October 2025, India approved an INR 15 billion incentive scheme for critical mineral recycling under the National Critical Mineral Mission. The scheme seeks to expand recycling capacity using processes such as hydrometallurgy, with incentives capped at INR 500 million for large recyclers and INR 250 million for small recyclers.

States such as Andhra Pradesh and Gujarat are also receiving support to build dedicated infrastructure for Critical Mineral Processing Parks, backed by an outlay of INR 5 billion. In addition, the basic customs duty on imported LIB scrap and capital goods used in processing has been withdrawn to lower the cost of securing feedstock and setting up recycling facilities.

Yet 75 percent of LIBs used in EVs come from China, with the import bill exceeding US$3 billion in FY2025. This dependence reflects India’s limited domestic capacity to manufacture battery materials and cells, with most existing capacity focused on assembling imported cells into battery packs.

Figure 3: Current Manufacturing Capacity and Additional Capacity Required by 2030

Note: Optimistic scenario: 1. Mobility: EV adoption exceeds targets, with overall EV new vehicle sales at 38% and very high penetration in 2- and 3-wheelers by 2030; 2. Stationary storage: 2-hour BESS is co-located with 100% of utility-scale solar and wind by 2030, while other storage uses remain as in the conservative case.

Conservative scenario: 1. Mobility: EVs reach 30% of new vehicle sales by 2030 with existing policy support; 2. Stationary storage: 2-hour BESS co-locates with 40% of new solar and wind capacity, focused on grid stability and peak management, with C&I storage largely excluded.

Source: Dalberg and Council for International Economic Understanding

The result is a persistent disconnect between growing domestic recycling capacity and the domestic manufacturing capacity required to absorb recovered materials into new batteries.

2. Battery-material and Cell Manufacturing

Domestic capacity for battery-material production is emerging. Altmin is developing India’s first LFP CAM facility in Telangana, while Himadri Speciality Chemical is expanding into LFP cathode and graphite-based anode materials, with plans to build an INR 300 billion battery business by around 2032.

Policy support for this segment is also developing, with the government considering an INR 130 billion incentive programme for advanced battery cell component makers covering CAMs, AAMs, electrolytes, separator film and copper foil, representing a more direct policy intervention.

Indirect support has also come through the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology’s (MeitY) Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme. It provides an additional 2 percent incentive over the turnover-linked incentive for domestic sourcing or manufacturing of CAMs for eligible digital applications. Under this initiative, MeitY approved an allocation of INR 145 crore in capital expenditure for Epsilon C2GR’s project for anode production in August 2026.

To develop domestic cell manufacturing, the Ministry of Heavy Industries approved the Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme in 2021, with a total outlay of INR 181 billion to establish 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity. Although it primarily incentivises cell manufacturing rather than battery materials, it adopts an evaluation framework that places considerable weight on domestic value addition (DVA), indirectly generating demand for locally produced battery materials.

However, this has yet to translate into expanding manufacturing capacity. India’s cell manufacturing reached only approximately 1 GWh by the end of 2025, and zero incentives had been disbursed to any beneficiary as of February 2026 due to non-fulfilment of the DVA requirements. While the ACC scheme seeks to deepen domestic linkages by rewarding higher levels of local value addition, such efforts remain uneven across the wider value chain.

Linking the Battery Value Chain

While recent regulatory measures and fiscal incentives are welcome developments, India risks growing dependence on imported battery inputs unless support for recycling, battery-material and cell manufacturing is coordinated.

Vertically integrated battery value chains in countries such as South Korea and China offer useful lessons in addressing this challenge. South Korea’s EcoPro ecosystem in Pohang co-locates recycling, lithium refining, precursor production and CAM manufacturing before returning to cell manufacturers. China’s CATL-Brunp model goes further, integrating mineral inputs, precursors, cathode materials, battery production and recycling within large industrial clusters. The lesson lies not simply in co-location, but in creating assured linkages between stages of the supply chain.

While recent regulatory measures and fiscal incentives are welcome developments, India risks growing dependence on imported battery inputs unless support for recycling, battery-material and cell manufacturing is coordinated.

For India, where capacity across streams is still developing, the policy priority should be to strengthen linkages through mechanisms such as long-term purchase agreements between recyclers and battery-material producers, supply agreements linking them to cell manufacturers, and incentives for using domestically recovered inputs under existing manufacturing schemes. Such measures could complement the BWM Rules, which require recycled materials to constitute 5 percent of the dry weight of new portable and EV batteries in FY2027-28, rising to 20 percent from FY2030-31.

The EPR framework provides a foundation for such interconnection. By placing responsibility for end-of-life batteries on producers and creating a market for recycling through registered recyclers, the framework already connects battery producers with the recycling segment. Integrated recyclers such as Lohum have built on this model by offering battery lifecycle-management services to Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), including recycling solutions that support compliance with EPR obligations.

Black mass recycling can help reduce India’s import dependence, but its contribution depends on whether recovered minerals re-enter domestic battery production.

Policy could build on this framework by extending incentives further along the value chain, encouraging recovered materials to flow from recyclers into domestic battery-material production and cell manufacturing.

Black mass recycling can help reduce India’s import dependence, but its contribution depends on whether recovered minerals re-enter domestic battery production. A targeted policy push is therefore needed to strengthen segment coordination, ensure offtake for recovered materials and build a circular battery supply chain.

Pranita Gupta is a Research Assistant with the Observer Research Foundation’s (ORF) Centre for Economy and Growth.

title: Senate Blocks Data Center Bill as AI Boom Reshapes U.S. Energy and Tech Markets

text:
Te FINANCIAL — The U.S. Senate on Sept. 17 blocked rapid passage of legislation that would require state regulators to consider making large data centers pay the full incremental cost of electricity infrastructure needed to serve them, one day after the House approved the measure 417-3.

The confrontation puts the physical infrastructure behind Artificial Intelligence at the center of a broader U.S. debate over electricity prices, grid expansion, water consumption, local development and the future location of data centers.

The House legislation, known as the Ratepayer Protection Act, was introduced by Rep. Gabe Evans, Republican of Colorado, and Rep. Kathy Castor, Democrat of Florida. Sen. Jon Husted, Republican of Ohio, brought the measure to the Senate floor on Sept. 17, seeking unanimous consent. Sen. Martin Heinrich, Democrat of New Mexico, objected, saying the House bill did not go far enough. The bill therefore did not advance through the expedited procedure.

The legislation would establish a federal standard for state utility regulators to consider when deciding how large electricity customers should pay for new generation, transmission, substations and distribution infrastructure. The House bill does not itself impose a mandatory national rate structure; it directs states and utilities to consider such standards.

The Senate dispute came after the House passed the measure by an overwhelming bipartisan margin. NBC News reported that President Donald Trump has supported the construction of new data centers as necessary infrastructure for U.S. Artificial Intelligence companies competing with China. At the same time, opposition to new facilities has grown in communities concerned about electricity, water, land use and environmental effects. The supplied NBC News report cited a September NBC News Decision Desk Poll in which nearly 70% of respondents opposed building AI data centers in their neighborhoods.

The data center boom is moving faster than the grid

The underlying economic trend is difficult to separate from AI.

The International Energy Agency reported that global data-center electricity consumption increased 17% in 2025, while electricity consumption from AI-focused data centers increased 50%. The IEA said capital expenditure by five major technology companies exceeded $400 billion in 2025 and was expected to rise another 75% in 2026.

In the United States, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s 2025 update estimates that data centers could consume 11.8% of total U.S. electricity by 2030, with a modeled range of 9.5% to 15.3%.

The Energy Information Administration’s 2026 outlook identifies data-center load as a major driver of U.S. electricity-demand growth. EIA forecasts U.S. electricity sales of 4,135 billion kilowatt-hours in 2026 and 4,211 billion in 2027.

The scale of the potential expansion varies substantially among forecasts because many announced data-center projects remain proposals rather than operating facilities.

Reuters reported in January that planned U.S. data-center capacity could theoretically increase from about 15 GW to more than 150 GW based on state and local filings, but noted that a significant portion of that pipeline is speculative.

Texas illustrates the size of the development pipeline. ERCOT reported more than 232,000 MW of large-load requests in its interconnection process in February 2026, with data centers accounting for the largest category in its reported project mix.

Where the next U.S. data centers are likely to be built

The established centers of the U.S. data-center economy remain important, but the geography is changing.

CBRE’s first-half 2026 research identifies Northern Virginia, Atlanta, Dallas-Fort Worth, Phoenix, Chicago, Silicon Valley, Hillsboro and the New York Tri-State region as the eight primary North American markets.

Northern Virginia remains the largest market by operating inventory. CBRE reported 4,496.5 MW of inventory in the first half of 2026, with vacancy at only 0.2%. But the market is increasingly constrained by power, land and permitting.

Atlanta moved ahead of Northern Virginia in construction activity, with about 2,882 MW under construction in the first half of 2026.

Dallas-Fort Worth is another major beneficiary. CBRE’s 2026 investor survey found that 78% of surveyed investors identified Dallas-Fort Worth among the most attractive markets, compared with 72% for Northern Virginia. Power availability, land, fiber infrastructure and Texas’ electricity-market structure were among the factors cited.

JLL’s midyear 2026 research shows an even broader geographic shift. It estimates that 77% of North American capacity under construction is now in so-called frontier markets. West Texas has been the largest beneficiary of this movement, while Ohio, Louisiana, Indiana and the Carolinas have also gained significant new development.

This does not mean established markets are disappearing. Instead, the industry is expanding into areas where developers can obtain large quantities of electricity and land without waiting years for constrained transmission systems to expand.

Data centers near New York

The New York Tri-State market remains a major data-center market but faces a different regulatory environment from Texas and parts of the South.

CBRE reported about 190 MW of inventory in the New York Tri-State market in the first half of 2026, considerably smaller than Northern Virginia, Atlanta and Dallas-Fort Worth.

New York State subsequently imposed a temporary halt on approvals for new data centers of 50 MW or more. The action demonstrates how power, environmental review and political considerations can become binding constraints even in regions with strong demand for digital infrastructure.

For developers, the New York area therefore presents a contrast with markets such as Texas and parts of the Southeast: access to customers and established network infrastructure is valuable, but the ability to obtain new power and permits can be more restrictive.

The New York data center market size stands at 854.5 MW in 2025 and is projected to reach 1,154.2 MW by 2031.

Key Market Statistics

Datacenters in Florida face a different resource equation

Florida is also becoming part of the national debate.

Florida’s 2026 legislation addressing large-scale data centers includes provisions concerning utility tariffs, grid reliability, water-use permits and foreign ownership restrictions involving countries designated as foreign countries of concern.

The legislation also calls for an independent study examining economic development, tax revenue, land, water and other natural resources, energy use, electricity-rate effects, and public health and safety associated with large-scale data centers.

Florida’s position is significant because the state’s electricity system must accommodate a combination of population growth, air-conditioning demand and new industrial loads while data centers can require unusually large, concentrated amounts of electricity.

Power, not land, may become the decisive resource

For years, the conventional data-center site-selection formula emphasized land, fiber connectivity, tax incentives and proximity to customers. CBRE’s 2026 research identifies power availability and infrastructure delivery timelines as the most decisive factors influencing site selection, leasing and pricing.

JLL similarly reports that power constraints are reshaping the development map.

The problem is partly physical. A large AI campus can require hundreds of megawatts or, in the largest cases, gigawatts of electricity. Serving such a facility can require generation, transmission lines, substations, transformers and distribution equipment.

FERC responded in June by ordering six regional grid operators to justify or reform their tariffs for data centers and other large energy users. The agency said the goal was to accelerate large-load interconnections while protecting reliability and consumers.

The result is a new infrastructure race involving utilities, gas turbines, nuclear generation, renewable power, batteries, transformers, switchgear, cooling systems and high-voltage transmission.

The corporations benefiting from the buildout

The beneficiaries extend well beyond Nvidia and other semiconductor companies.

Nvidia remains one of the clearest examples. The company reported $89 billion in data-center revenue for its fiscal second quarter of 2027, up 117% from a year earlier.

But the data-center economy increasingly includes several layers.

Hyperscalers: Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle are among the largest purchasers and operators of AI infrastructure.

Semiconductors: Nvidia and other chip suppliers benefit from the continuing deployment of accelerators, networking hardware and memory.

Power equipment: Eaton and GE Vernova have reported substantial demand associated with electricity infrastructure. Eaton said its Electrical Americas orders rose 42% on a rolling 12-month basis, citing data-center momentum. GE Vernova reported $2.4 billion of Electrification orders for data centers in the first quarter of 2026, more than the entire amount booked during 2025.

Backup generation: Generac signed a long-term agreement with Amazon worth about $2.4 billion for initial generator deliveries in 2027 and 2028, with the overall arrangement potentially reaching $8 billion. Generac shares rose sharply after the announcement.

Utilities: Dominion Energy, Duke Energy, Southern Company, NextEra Energy, Vistra and other electricity companies are positioned to benefit from additional generation and grid investment, although they also face regulatory risks if consumers or regulators resist cost allocation.

Construction and real estate: Data-center developers, engineering companies, contractors, commercial landlords and infrastructure investors are receiving a growing share of the capital flowing into AI infrastructure.

Meta, for example, announced a venture with BlackRock and affiliated infrastructure investors to develop a data-center campus in El Paso, Texas.

The expansion has also created a financing market around data centers. JLL reported $17 billion of combined SASB/CMBS and ABS data-center financing volume during the first half of 2026.

What is critical inside an AI data center?

The modern AI data center is increasingly a power-and-cooling facility wrapped around computing hardware.

The critical components include:

Electricity generation and grid connection

High-voltage transmission

Substations and transformers

Power distribution and backup systems

AI accelerators and high-bandwidth memory

Fiber-optic connectivity

Liquid and advanced cooling systems

Backup generators and batteries

Water supply or water-efficient cooling

Physical security and cybersecurity

Land with appropriate zoning

Skilled construction and technical labor

Cooling is particularly important because AI processors generate much more heat at high utilization than conventional enterprise servers.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory research published in 2025 found that workload-level water consumption can vary by more than 10,000-fold. Server efficiency, grid water intensity, utilization, cooling technology, infrastructure efficiency and climate are among the factors determining water requirements.

What research says about health effects

The scientific literature requires a distinction between documented environmental exposures and proven long-term health outcomes.

A 2025 paper in Eco-Environment & Health called for substantially more empirical research into the health effects of data-center expansion. The authors identified several potential exposure pathways, including noise from cooling equipment and backup generators, air pollution from fossil-fuel generation and diesel generators, and localized water stress.

A 2026 exploratory assessment published in Frontiers in Climate similarly reviewed potential health pathways involving air pollution, water consumption, noise, land-use changes and economic effects in Virginia.

However, researchers emphasize that direct epidemiological evidence linking data-center operations to long-term health outcomes in surrounding populations remains limited.

That distinction matters.

There is strong evidence that exposure to air pollution and excessive environmental noise can affect human health generally. What remains less established is the precise magnitude of those effects attributable specifically to data centers and their associated electricity infrastructure.

A 2025 study by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that data-center water consumption depends heavily on facility design and location. A 2026 paper in AGU Advances concluded that localized water impacts can be significant, particularly in drought-prone or water-stressed regions, while calling for greater transparency around facility-level water use.

Which regions outside the U.S. benefit from America’s data-center investment?

Taiwan is particularly important because of its position in advanced semiconductor manufacturing.

South Korea is also expanding its role in the AI infrastructure chain. Reuters reported Sept. 18 that the United States and South Korea were discussing major investments in U.S. power and nuclear projects, including a proposed 6.3-GW gas-fired power plant in Texas intended to supply AI and semiconductor facilities.

Japan is another major source of capital. The U.S. Commerce Department has announced Japan-U.S. strategic investments involving natural-gas generation and potential small modular reactor projects. Reporting has linked Japanese capital to power infrastructure intended to support U.S. AI facilities.

Mexico can benefit through electronics manufacturing and cross-border industrial supply chains, while Vietnam and other Asian economies can benefit through components, electronics and semiconductor-related exports.

The flow is therefore two-directional: the United States is attracting enormous capital into physical AI infrastructure, while foreign economies supply many of the chips, electronics and industrial components required to build it.

The United States is not the only country building for AI

Foreign competition may also influence where U.S. investment ultimately goes.

PwC’s 2026 Global Data Centre Outlook projects $31.6 trillion of cumulative AI-infrastructure capital expenditure through 2050, with the United States expected to capture about $15.1 trillion, or 48%, under its baseline scenario.

JLL expects global data-center capacity to roughly double between 2026 and 2030.

Europe, Asia and the Middle East are simultaneously pursuing sovereign AI infrastructure to reduce dependence on U.S. and Chinese computing platforms.

Canada is building its own AI infrastructure. The Canadian government announced in September that Bell Canada planned an AI infrastructure expansion in Saskatchewan that could provide up to 900 MW of new capacity, with a potential 1.2-GW AI hub.

South Korea has announced an even larger domestic AI infrastructure strategy, with its science ministry saying the country intends to invest more than $650 billion in AI data centers through 2035.

The consequence is that U.S. leadership in AI does not eliminate international competition for capital, electricity, chips and computing capacity.

How the Senate bill could affect technology stocks

The Ratepayer Protection Act creates several possible financial effects, but its ultimate market impact cannot be known from the Senate vote alone.

If similar requirements eventually become law, the immediate effect would be to shift more infrastructure costs toward large data-center operators and away from existing electricity customers.

For hyperscalers such as Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle, that could increase the capital cost of new facilities in regions where utilities currently socialize some infrastructure expenses.

For utilities, the effect could be different. Requiring large customers to provide greater financial assurance or pay incremental infrastructure costs could reduce the risk that utilities invest in generation or transmission that later becomes stranded if a data-center project is canceled.

For equipment suppliers, increased spending on substations, transformers, generators, switchgear, cooling systems and transmission could increase demand even if the bill slows some data-center projects.

The strongest near-term stock-market evidence comes from individual corporate announcements rather than the legislation itself. Generac’s shares rose sharply after its Amazon agreement was announced. Eaton and GE Vernova have also reported strong data-center-related orders.

But the Senate’s Sept. 17 action does not establish a new nationwide cost regime. The House legislation was blocked from passage in the Senate, and the House version itself would have required states to consider standards rather than automatically imposing a single federal tariff.

Therefore, the effect on Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Oracle, utilities and infrastructure suppliers depends on whether Congress ultimately passes legislation, what provisions survive, and how individual states implement large-load rules.

Northern Virginia remains the largest U.S. data-center market, while Atlanta, Texas, the Midwest, Pennsylvania, Louisiana, Indiana and the Carolinas are attracting new projects. New York remains strategically important but faces tighter regulatory constraints. Florida is developing its own framework for electricity, water and large-scale data centers.

The underlying competition is increasingly not simply over who has the best AI model.

text:
Nearly 3,000 acres of Ohio’s only national forest were leased this week for more than $11 million by the Bureau of Land Management to out-of-state companies for fracking.

The BLM auctioned off 40 parcels in Monroe and Washington counties totaling 2,776 acres in Wayne National Forest for $11.09 million during a quarterly oil and gas lease sale.

“Leasing is the first step in the process to develop federal oil and gas resources,” BLM said in a statement.

“The BLM ensures oil and gas development meets the requirements set forth by the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 and other applicable legal authorities. Oil and gas leases are awarded for a term of 10 years and as long thereafter as there is production of oil and gas in paying quantities.”

These are the companies that are leasing the parcels:

Pennsylvania-based Apex Energy Operating III LLC leased 25 parcels for $7.97 million.

Texas-based R&R Royalty LTD leased six parcels for $864,234.

Oklahoma-based Gulfport Appalachia LLC leased five parcels for $1.98 million.

Texas-based Texas Independent Exploration Limited leased three parcels for $241,559.

Pennsylvania-based Ohio Gasco LLC leased one parcel for $25,769.

The BLM scoped out the parcels in January and announced the auction in July.

Fracking is the process of injecting liquid into the ground at a high pressure to extract oil or gas.

Nathan Johnson, senior attorney for the Ohio Environmental Council, said the lease sale violates important environmental laws meant to protect endangered wildlife and the quality of the environment.

“The Wayne is Ohio’s only National Forest and one of the state’s best places for outdoor recreation,” Johnson said. “Fracking the Wayne will pollute the air, harm local streams, and industrialize the landscape. We are preparing to challenge yesterday’s leasing in federal court.”

The Wayne National Forest was established in 1935 and totals 244,000 acres spanning 12 counties with three units in Athens, Ironton, and Marietta in Southeast Ohio.

More than 200,000 people visit Wayne National Forest annually, which is known for its hiking, biking, horseback riding trails, and off-road vehicle trails.

Spending by visitors to the Wayne National Forest is about $7.4 million annually, according to the United States Forest Service.

This is the first lease sale in Wayne National Forest since March 2017 when 20 parcels in Monroe County were auctioned off.

A national forest is managed by the U.S. Forest Service under the Department of Agriculture and blends conservation with public service and resource extraction like logging and mining.

Wayne National Forest already has 1,200 conventional wells, but the BLM predicts new wells drilled in the Wayne will be horizontal, hydraulic fracturing natural-gas wells.

There were approximately 2,000 incidents associated with oil and gas wells in Ohio from 2015-2023 — including 98 incidents in Monroe County and 85 incidents in Washington counties, according to FracTracker Alliance, a nonprofit that collects data on fracking pipelines.

Washington County residents have been raising concerns that injection wells leaking brine waste could contaminate Marietta’s drinking water.

Evidence shows increased exposure to fracking impacts health, in particular children’s health, including low birth weight, preterm births, congenital anomalies, and asthma, according to Yale School of Medicine.

title: WV power providers fight 'public interest' reform, work to extend coal plant lives
authors: Mike Tony, PERRY BENNETT, W.Va. Legislative Photography
description: West Virginians have had to contend with some of the region’s highest electricity bills amid the state’s nation-highest dependence on coal-fired power. West Virginia’s average monthly residential electric bill of $154.76 in 2024 was higher than all 12 other states in the PJM Interconnection LLC regional electric grid except Maryland, per U.S. Energy Information Administration data — 8.8% higher than the national average of $142.26. Mountain State ratepayers have been on the hook for increasingly costly upgrades at the in-state coal-fired plants operated by subsidiaries of American Electric Power and FirstEnergy. Throughout the country, wear-and-tear-saddled coal plants have struggled to maintain reliability during weather emergencies and peak demand times as coal itself has become more expensive compared with alternative energy sources. A meeting of West Virginia lawmakers on Sept. 15, 2026 shed light on a key administrative power struggle behind state ratepayers’ electric power struggle and indicated the state is poised to keep relying on coal for decades to come – as American Electric Power Service Corp. and FirstEnergy fight a key market reform recommended by consumer advocates.

WASHINGTON – Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), a lifelong family farmer and member of the Senate Agriculture Committee, accepted Growth Energy’s 2026 “Fueling Growth Award” for his leadership on biofuels and his ongoing support for America’s family farmers and biofuel producers.

“As a lifelong Iowa corn and soybean farmer, I know firsthand how important our homegrown biofuels are for our national security, our pocketbooks and our environment. Biofuels are good, good, good. That’s why I’m continuing to fight tirelessly to get year-round, nationwide E15 over the finish line,” Grassley said. “I’m proud to be a strong voice for Iowa biofuels at the policymaking tables in Washington.”

Senator Grassley accepts the 2026 "Fueling Growth Award" from members of Growth Energy, including Iowa family farmer and biofuels advocate Bill Couser.

Download photo HERE.

Background:

Grassley helped establish the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) in the Energy Policy Act of 2005, and conducts oversight to ensure the executive branch appropriately implements the program.

Grassley also met with the National Oilseed Association yesterday to discuss the RFS. The group presented Grassley with an award recognizing him as a Champion of Agriculture.

Grassley has championed E15 in the Senate for over 15 years:

April 2026: Spoke on the Senate floor to support Iowa’s Members of Congress for fighting for family farmers on E15 and the Farm Bill.

March 2026: Spoke at an Agriculture Committee hearing in strong support of E15.

January 2026: Wrote an op-ed praising President Trump’s support for legislation allowing for the year-round, nationwide sale of E15.

September 2025: Received Growth Energy’s 2025 “Fueling Growth Award” for his efforts to support biofuel production.

October 2025: Called for any legislation that includes ad hoc payments to farmers to also include E15.

August 2025: Introduced the bipartisan Ethanol for America Act to make it easier for Americans to fuel their vehicles with homegrown E15.

April 2025: Joined a bipartisan letter urging President Trump to permit the nationwide sale of E15 fuel through the 2025 summer driving season and beyond.

February 2025: Reintroduced the Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act with Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.), a congressional proposal to allow for E15 sales year-round and nationwide.

April 2024: Welcomed the EPA’s emergency fuel waiver permitting nationwide E15 sales for the summer 2024 driving season.

February 2024: Applauded the EPA’s decision to approve a petition from eight Midwestern governors to permanently authorize year-round E-15 sales in their states.

text:
The city of West Lafayette has received the 2026 Governor’s Award for Environmental Excellence for a solar energy project that expanded renewable power generation at municipal facilities.

The award, presented by the Indiana Department of Environmental Management, recognizes projects that provide measurable environmental, economic and social benefits, according to a community announcement. The city said it added more than 315 kilowatts of rooftop solar capacity in 2025 through installations at four municipal buildings and the West Lafayette Public Library.

The project expanded the city’s renewable energy use, reduced environmental impacts and is expected to help lower long-term operating costs.

“This initiative demonstrates how sustainability can benefit both our environment and city operations,” said Clara Lotz, climate resiliency & sustainability officer. “We are extremely proud to be recognized by IDEM for our work in renewable energy and to see the benefits this project is providing through cost savings, educational opportunities, and community partnerships.”

Mayor Erin R. Easter said the award reflects the city's commitment to environmental stewardship and long-term planning.

“This recognition reflects the kind of thoughtful, long-term investments we want to make in West Lafayette,” Easter said. “Environmental stewardship is a responsibility we take seriously, and this project shows how we can put that commitment into action while making responsible use of public resources. I’m proud of the collaboration that made this work possible and proud to see West Lafayette recognized at the state level.”

Solar expansion financed through redevelopment program

The West Lafayette Redevelopment Commission financed the rooftop solar initiative with Tax Increment Financing funds.

City officials said the project also qualified for a 30% federal clean energy tax credit available through the Inflation Reduction Act. More information is available at irs.gov.

The 2025 installations were completed at:

Fire Station 3

John R. Dennis Wellness Center

Margerum City Hall

Street and Sanitation

West Lafayette Public Library

Solar project tied to emissions goals

SolarEdge estimates that cumulative energy production from West Lafayette’s municipal solar systems has prevented more than 2.2 million pounds of carbon dioxide emissions.

The figure includes output from an earlier solar installation completed at the John R. Dennis Wellness Center in 2020 as well as the systems added in 2025.

According to the announcement, the added solar capacity supports a regional goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 58% by 2030 under the Greater Lafayette Climate Action Plan. Additional information about the plan is available at greaterlafayetteind.com.

The city said the effort involved coordination among municipal departments, the West Lafayette Public Library and project partners including the West Lafayette Redevelopment Commission, Solar Energy Systems, Duke Energy, Be Represented and Baker Tilly.

text:
National Assembly Holds Seminar on September 18 As China Expands Low-Price EV Exports, Saying China’s Low-Cost Push Threatens Domestic Auto Base

Amid the intensifying low-price offensive by Chinese companies in the global electric vehicle market, voices have emerged stating that it is urgent to prepare comprehensive government-level support measures to protect the production base and secure the competitiveness of the domestic automobile industry.

The National Assembly Mobility Forum, a research group of lawmakers, held its second seminar of 2026 under the theme of ‘Measures to Strengthen the Competitiveness of the Domestic Electric Vehicle Industry’ at the National Assembly Members’ Office Building in Yeouido, Seoul, on the morning of Sept. 18.

At this seminar, hosted by the National Assembly Mobility Forum and co-organized by the Korea Automobile and Mobility Association (KAMA) and the Korean Society of Mobility, participants analyzed China’s overseas expansion strategies and extensively discussed tax, legislative, and industrial policy tasks to strengthen the domestic production base.

Intensifying Global EV Hegemony War and the Reality of South Korea

Recently, the global electric vehicle market has been transitioning beyond competition among individual companies into a pattern of industrial competition between countries, combining government support, trade policies, production bases, and supply chains. Chinese electric vehicle companies, which have grown amid active support from the Chinese government, are rapidly expanding their market influence by putting forward low prices and overseas local production systems.

In response, major automobile producing countries are reinforcing measures to protect their domestic industries in all directions. The United States is imposing high tariffs of up to 127.5% on Chinese electric vehicles, and the European Union (EU) has also decided to apply tariffs of up to 45.3% on Chinese battery electric vehicles. Japan is also focusing its efforts on securing the competitiveness of its domestic industry by significantly strengthening support policies linked to the domestic production of batteries and electric vehicles, as well as providing purchase support and expanding charging infrastructure.

On the other hand, South Korea has no other countermeasures other than a basic tariff of 8% on Chinese electric vehicles, raising concerns about the contraction of the domestic production base.

“Urgent Need to Introduce Domestic Production Tax Credit and Support the Ecosystem”

On this day, the attendees voiced in unison that tax support linked to domestic production and the comprehensive strengthening of the industrial ecosystem must be swiftly promoted to protect the domestic production base against the low-price offensive, and proactive movements by the government are also being detected.

Co-representative of the National Assembly Mobility Forum, Representative Yoon Hoo-duk, emphasized that a domestic production tax credit, including for electric vehicles, is a core task to protect employment and the regional economy by directly supporting domestic production and parts demand. Co-representative, Representative Yoon Han-hong, introduced that he had proposed an amendment to the Restriction of Special Taxation Act encompassing electric vehicles in August, and expressed his will to do his best in support legislation and regulatory improvement covering not only the production tax credit but also technology development, supply chains, and charging infrastructure in the future.

Research Director Representative Bae June-young suggested that legislative policies are needed to strongly support the overall industrial ecosystem, including batteries, core parts, charging infrastructure, safety, and supply chains, while President of the Korea Automobile and Mobility Association Jeong Dae-jin urged that since there is a limit to responding to the low-price offensive of Chinese products solely through corporate efforts, a production tax credit, R&D and facility investment support, and the strengthening of the core supply chain must be comprehensively promoted.

As the recent candidate for Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyung-il revealed his intention to collect opinions from the industry, there is an atmosphere of rising expectations that discussions on introducing a tax credit for electric vehicle production will further accelerate.

In the subsequent topic presentation, KAIST Professor Park Jung-gyu reviewed the current status of the Chinese electric vehicle industry and its overseas expansion strategies, and Korea Automobile and Mobility Association Managing Director Yoon Kyung-sun expressed the necessity of production-linked support systems including the domestic production tax credit, R&D and facility investment support, strengthening of the core supply chain, and support for stable demand creation.

Finally, in the designated discussion moderated by President of the Korean Society of Mobility Jeong Gu-min, officials from related ministries such as the Ministry of Finance and Economy, the Ministry of Trade and Industry, and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, as well as experts from the National Assembly Research Service and the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade, participated in large numbers to discuss specific tax, industrial, and transportation policies and legislative tasks to strengthen the competitiveness of the domestic electric vehicle industry from various angles.

The National Assembly Mobility Forum plans to actively continue legislative and institutional improvement activities to maintain the domestic electric vehicle production base and technological competitiveness based on the voices from the field and expert opinions presented on this day.

text:
Red E Charge is adding a nice convenience feature at its EV chargers across the United States.

After an initial account setup, drivers will no longer need a physical credit card or the company’s smartphone app to charge.

Red E Charge was one of the fastest-growing DC fast charging networks in the second quarter, ahead of Electrify America, EVgo, and Ionna.

It just got a little easier to top up your EV’s battery at Red E Charge stations across the United States. The Detroit-based company, which was one of the fastest-growing DC charging networks in the country in the second quarter, has enabled Plug & Charge functionality at many of its dispensers.

With Plug & Charge, EV drivers need to complete a one-time setup in the charging network’s smartphone app, adding details about their vehicle and a payment method. After the setup is complete, they can simply plug in and charge at compatible stations, with the payment being handled automatically. No more scanning QR codes, opening an app, or getting out a credit card.

The operator has dubbed this service Red E Go, saying that the feature is available at certain stations. Currently, the network has over 1,000 locations and roughly 4,600 charging ports across 46 American states, according to the Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels Data Center. Out of the total, 2,159 ports offer fast charging at 579 stations, with 600 of the locations also offering almost 2,500 Level 2 charging ports.

On the DC charging side, Red E was the fourth fastest-growing network in the country in the second quarter of this year, according to a Paren report. With 315 new ports, Red E ranked below Tesla, Walmart, and ChargePoint, but overtook Electrify America, EVgo, and Ionna.

What’s more, Red E’s customers are quite happy with the charging experience. The network ranked fifth in terms of overall satisfaction in JD Power’s latest Electric Vehicle Experience (EVX) Public Charging Study, after Ionna, the Mercedes-Benz Charging Network, the Rivian Adventure Network, and Tesla’s Supercharger network. With 628 points on a 1,000-point scale, Red E was just below the 666-point segment average, but higher than Electrify America, EVgo, and ChargePoint.

The power output of Red E’s stalls ranges from just 10 kilowatts to a rather impressive 640 kilowatts, depending on the location and plug type. The network offers J1772, CCS1, NACS, and CHAdeMO plugs, with prices ranging from $0.40/kilowatt-hour to $1.15/kWh, according to DCFC Tracker.

text:
Volvo is planning its biggest-ever product offensive, including seven new cars for Western markets, as it adopts a more flexible approach to electrification and prepares to rethink its interiors.

The Swedish brand plans to launch 13 new electrified cars - globally - by the end of 2030 as part of a major strategic reset that will provide a broader range of vehicles for fleets and company car drivers. Saloons and estates could make a comeback, as part of the new line-up.

The plan, announced at Volvo Cars’ Strategy Update in Stockholm on 17 September, includes seven new models for Western markets and six for China, with a combination of electric vehicles (EVs) and third-generation plug-in hybrids (PHEVs).

Earlier this week, Volvo announced a new long-range PHEV system for the XC60 and XC90. The new powertrain enables an electric range of up to 124 miles in the XC60 and 99 miles in XC90. They will be available early next year.

It also revealed a facelifted version of the XC40.

Volvo said the strategy is designed to respond to "different customer preferences and market conditions", rather than pursuing the same product strategy globally. It is targeting an EBIT margin of more than 8% in the long term, up from 3.5% in 2025, while aiming to double its market share.

While company car taxation continues to favour zero-emission models, with a 4% benefit-in-kind (BiK) rate for EVs in 2026/27, long-range PHEVs still provide an affordable option for drivers who may not yet be able to rely entirely on public or home charging.

Volvo has already adjusted its previous ambition of becoming fully electric by 2030. Its current target is for 90-100% of global sales to be electrified by 2030, including EVs and PHEVs, with a limited role for mild hybrids if required.

More choice for fleets

Volvo said the seven Western-market models it plans to launch will use its existing SPA2 and SPA3 architectures and HuginCore computing platform, reducing the investment required for each new vehicle.

It also expects greater collaboration with Geely to deliver cost savings, targeting around 30% commonality in parts by 2030, compared with 10% today. Volvo estimates this could reduce material costs by around 5%.

For European customers, Volvo's design team is also examining how regionalisation could influence the shape of its cars. Design chief Thomas Ingenlath, who recently returned to the brand from Polestar, has indicated that Europe could see more focus on lower-slung models such as saloons and estates, in contrast to the larger vehicles being prioritised for North America.

That could give Volvo a broader offering for the company-car market, where premium saloons and estates have traditionally played an important role alongside SUVs.

Ensure you always get Fleet News insight. Make us your preferred source on Google

Physical controls set to return

The strategy announcement also contained a significant change in Volvo's interior philosophy.

Ingenlath said the brand needs to find a better balance between touchscreen interfaces and physical interaction.

He criticised the industry's increasing reliance on screens and said Volvo was listening to customers and journalists who have complained about screen-heavy interiors. Future Volvos will retain touchscreens, but the brand intends to bring back a limited number of physical controls for functions where tactile interaction makes more sense.

Importantly, Ingenlath said Volvo would not simply recreate older dashboards packed with switches. Instead, controls could have different physical forms – such as clicks, twists or other tactile interactions – to make them more intuitive and enhance the sense of quality inside the car.

The first indication of this new design philosophy is expected in a new concept car due to be shown in 2027, Volvo's centenary year.

Volvo is also changing how it views the customer relationship, moving from simply selling cars towards a wider offer built around software, Volvo ID, Care subscriptions and ongoing digital services.
