text:
A new analysis of U.S. electric vehicle sales projects that a record share of new vehicles sold in 2030 will be electric, despite recent steps by the federal government to remove incentives to their growth.

The report, by researchers at the Salata Institute for Climate and Sustainability, indicates that EVs will make up an estimated 32 percent of new car sales by 2030 — assuming current policy remains in place — quadruple the 8 percent share of new sales in 2025.

That forecast does not mean the steps taken by the current administration, which opposes federal support for EVs, are having no impact. The researchers pointed out that absent those steps EVs would make up an even greater share of 2030 new car sales, as high as an estimated 48 percent.

“In the long run, everything’s going in the direction of market-based adoption, despite the moves by the Trump administration that reduce pressure for EV sales,” said Elaine Buckberg, senior fellow at the Salata Institute, at the Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs, and one of the report’s authors.

The report, “Simulating Impacts of Proposed Trump Policy Changes on Electric Vehicle (EV) Adoption,” was released in July and written by Buckberg, James Stock, the Harold Hitchings Burbank Professor of Political Economy, and by former Ph.D. student in economics Cassandra Cole.

The work analyzed the impact of several regulatory and legislative steps taken by the government since January 2025 that have removed tax credits for EV sales and the installation of new charging equipment, eliminated restrictions on tailpipe emissions, and revoked California’s ability to impose stricter tailpipe emission standards than the federal government requires, among others.

Several of these moves are being challenged in court.

The researchers modeled the impact of each of the steps, with the largest being removing the purchase tax credit, which cut up to $7,500 off the price of a new electric vehicle and alone accounts for an estimated 6.2 percentage point reduction in EVs’ share of 2030 new vehicle sales.

The step would also save the government $169.2 billion in lost revenue from the tax credits over the decade spanning 2026 and 2035.

Buckberg, former chief economist for General Motors, said the analysis shows the administration’s moves will slow but not stop an expected acceleration in EV adoption. The most immediate reason for this is that many prospective buyers, while happy for the tax credit, would buy the cars even without it.

Perhaps more significant in the long term are broader changes that make EVs increasingly competitive with gasoline vehicles. Chief among them are advances in battery technology, which will allow automakers to offer longer-range EVs without increasing price.

Along with those changes have come shifts in how EV owners use their vehicles.

Increasingly, Buckberg said, electric vehicles have greater range and can be recharged more rapidly on the road. That means that, while early adopters often used them as a second vehicle, mainly around town, EV owners today are often using them in much the same way they would gasoline-powered vehicles.

The biggest hurdle to adoption is consumer concern about charging infrastructure, Buckberg said. As that infrastructure grows nationally, gaps in charger coverage will narrow.

What will help, Buckberg said, is making charger status and price available so EV drivers can find them in any mapping app. By reducing consumer “range anxiety,” app-data transparency alone could potentially boost sales 6 percent.

“Concerns about charging are the biggest holdback to EV adoption,” Buckberg said. “If we continue to see improvements in battery cost and battery density translating to EV prices, when it becomes price equivalent or very close it becomes much more attractive. If you are doing a road trip, you have at least 300 miles of range and can go to a highway charger that takes 10 to 15 minutes, it becomes a more perfect substitute.”

As EVs approach price parity with internal combustion vehicles — which has occurred with some models — other advantages of electric vehicles will carry greater weight with the consumer, Buckberg said. Among them are better performance, a reduction in routine maintenance needs as EVs have fewer moving parts, and insulation from the price swings of gasoline.

“The EV tax credit — one of the things that’s gotten the most focus — will become less and less relevant as the price gap narrows,” Buckberg said. “Our research shows that charging is by far the most cost-effective lever. Real-time data is the least expensive lever of all, and something states can act on right now.”

With U.S. carmakers also competing internationally, another important development has been the growth of EV sales worldwide.

The International Energy Agency, in its July report on the global outlook for EVs, said that sales worldwide are ahead of those in the U.S. and expected to reach 29 percent of global car sales this year, up 10 percent over 2025.

Increased electric car sales come at a time when overall car sales have declined globally.

Buckberg said the global embrace of EVs has been boosted in part by the war with Iran, its disruption of oil supplies, and the increased prices that come with it.

The IEA report, in fact, said that sales in Australia, Brazil, India, Korea, and Vietnam have approximately doubled since the global energy crisis began, measured from March to June 2026 versus 2025.

“EV adoption is rising,” Buckberg said. “In 2025, there were 25 markets where EV sales topped 10 percent and there were about a dozen where it topped 20 percent.”

text:
Investors following legacy automakers as the globe transitions to electric vehicles (EVs) might have identified a big opportunity with Stellantis (STLA +2.64%). While Detroit rivals Ford Motor Company (F +1.95%) and General Motors (GM +2.76%) have both traded about 5% higher year to date, Stellantis fell off a cliff with a 51% decline. However, with Stellantis putting up a massive $70 billion turnaround plan, it may have the most upside of all three over the next five years. If we zero in on Stellantis' profit engine, its North America region, it has an interesting strategy of what segments it will attack and what products, especially considering its pullback on less profitable EVs, the $25 billion investment could pay off huge.

North America or bust

Stellantis' $70 billion global "FaSTLAne 2030" plan has a plethora of moving parts and regional strategies stretching across the globe, and all will play their own role in the broader turnaround. However, one make-or-break region for the success of its overall turnaround will absolutely be North America, which has remained the company's profit engine since Fiat Chrysler Automobiles and PSA Group merged 50-50, combining 14 historical auto brands from the U.S., Italy, and France.

North America is so important to Stellantis' turnaround that its committing 60% of all brand and product investments from its overall plan directly to North America. Those funds will help develop and launch 11 all-new vehicles, expanding its market coverage by a staggering 50%. Stellantis is taking a calculated approach to exactly how it's attacking new North American segments, and it could make all the difference.

Where is the capital going?

On one end of the spectrum, Stellantis is introducing nine vehicles priced under $40,000, providing some relief to pent-up demand for more affordable vehicles as the average price of new vehicles remains near record highs at around $50,000. Stellantis is also planning to use its Chrysler brand as a more regional path to offering even more affordable vehicles, including two priced below $30,000.

On the other end of the spectrum, Stellantis is also using its popular Jeep and Ram brands to pinpoint more lucrative segments with performance models and all-new products. These are arguably the two most important brands in all of Stellantis' global turnaround. One example of where the investment could pay off big is Ram's first-ever SUV, moving into brand-new territory while reviving its historic Ramcharger nameplate. Ram is also looking to expand beyond its historical "full-size-only" focus with the Rampage, a new compact pickup truck, and by reviving the highly anticipated Dakota midsize truck. Not to be left behind, Jeep gets attention in the form of a $600 million investment to reopen a Belvidere Assembly Plant in Illinois which will increase production of the next-generation Jeep Compass and bring back the Jeep Cherokee. Furthermore, Jeep's core product portfolio will undergo a complete overhaul by the end of this decade, with a complete redesign of the Wrangler SUV and Gladiator pickup, refreshed Grand Cherokee and Grand Wagoneer, and a rebooted Street and Racing Technology (SRT) division.

What it all means

Here's the good news, as well as the catch: Stellantis' use of Chrysler and other more affordable models to attack the affordability crisis happening in the U.S. auto market is a brilliant way to increase sales volume and production capacity utilization. The catch is that Stellantis will have work to do on its value strategy and cost-cutting to ensure these vehicles remain profitable, or the turnaround will lose steam.

By Comms Team | Published on 17 September 2026 | 4 min read

Pre-cast tunnel segments and heads to be transported to Suffolk by rail and sea

Facility builds on the positive legacy left by Hinkley Point C

Employment and Skills plan to support apprentices and work experience students

Sizewell C has secured planning permission for a major tunnel production facility in Avonmouth, supporting up to 400 jobs and strengthening the UK’s nuclear supply chain.

The facility will manufacture the pre-cast concrete segments and tunnel heads needed to construct Sizewell C’s marine tunnels. Once complete, the components will be transported to Suffolk by rail and sea, supporting the project’s commitment to move at least 60% of construction materials by rail and sea, significantly reducing the need for HGVs to travel on local roads.

Located around 10 kilometres north-west of Bristol city centre, the development builds on the successful tunnel production facility delivered at the same site for Hinkley Point C, Sizewell C’s sister project. Drawing on proven expertise and innovation, it will help sustain and create skilled jobs while leaving a lasting legacy of engineering and manufacturing capability across the South West.

Nigel Cann, CEO of Sizewell C, said: “Opening this facility and supporting hundreds of jobs at Bristol Port shows once again that Sizewell C is delivering growth and opportunities right across the UK.

“Manufacturing our pre-cast concrete components off-site and delivering them by rail and sea means the benefits will be felt in our host community too – with less construction traffic on local roads.

“It’s also another great example of how we’re using the learnings from Hinkley Point C, which has seen significant advancements through off-site prefabrication, and taking them to the next level. By reusing existing infrastructure and experienced teams, we can reap the benefits across safety, quality, cost, and schedule.”

Expanding the existing site includes building temporary supporting infrastructure such as concrete batching plants, cranes, offices, welfare facilities, storage areas and parking.

Early works are already underway. A total of 55 people, the vast majority from the Avonmouth area, are employed by Sizewell C’s delivery partner, the Civil Works Alliance (CWA), including two apprentices and a summer work experience placement. A further 86 supply chain workers are currently on site.

Subject to conditions being met, production of the tunnel segments and heads are expected to begin in 2028.

Michael Mitchell, who worked at Avonmouth for HPC as a Site Engineer for four years, said: “I am excited about the opportunity to contribute to another major infrastructure development and look forward to the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead. I am particularly grateful to be involved in such a significant project while also being able to return home to my family each day, achieving a much better work-life balance.”

An Employment and Skills Plan will be delivered by the CWA in partnership with local authorities, education providers and industry partners to maximise opportunities for local people. The programme will focus on:

Promoting careers in construction, engineering and the nuclear sector through engagement with local schools.

Expanding access to apprenticeships, work experience placements, internships, graduate programmes and vocational training.

Supporting under-represented groups and those facing barriers to employment.

Daniel Altier, CWA Marine and Tunnelling Delivery Director, said: “The CWA is committed to not only establishing a state-of-the-art factory that will manufacture the 38,500 segments required for the three tunnels, but also to train a skilled workforce, with the majority coming from the local area.”

The investment in Avonmouth further strengthens the UK’s advanced manufacturing capability while supporting the delivery of one of the country’s most important clean energy projects and providing employment opportunities across the UK.

Darren Jones, MP for Bristol North West, said: “Last June, the government announced £14.2 billion investment to build the Sizewell C nuclear plant, with nuclear power to play an important role in strengthening the UK’s energy security as we transition to clean energy. The investment will create thousands of jobs across the country, and I’m delighted to hear that a sizeable number of these Sizewell C skilled jobs are coming to Avonmouth in my constituency.”

The announcement also builds on Sizewell C’s growing economic contribution across the UK. The project’s second Annual Sustainability Report revealed that almost £5bn has already been invested with more than 1,000 UK suppliers, including around £1bn with businesses in Suffolk.

text:
H.J.Res.213 passed the House on Wednesday, 210 Republicans and three Democrats in favour

Targets the EPA waiver behind the Commercial Harbor Craft rule, which has put California tugs and ferries on renewable diesel since 2023

Follows Tuesday's 216-211 vote against the At-Berth shore power rule

Campaign group Pacific Environment calls on the Senate to block both; operators say the rule's diesel filter requirement is unworkable

The US House of Representatives has voted to overturn the federal waiver behind California's Commercial Harbor Craft rule, the regulation that has required tugs, ferries, and other workboats in the state to run on renewable diesel since 2023.

House Joint Resolution 213, sponsored by California Republican James Gallagher, passed 214 to 208 on Wednesday evening, with three Democrats joining 210 Republicans and one independent in favour, according to the House Clerk's record.

It came a day after the House voted 216 to 211 to overturn the At-Berth shore power rule, and both resolutions now go to the Senate, where Ohio Republican Bernie Moreno has filed the harbor craft companion and a simple majority is enough.

Both use the Congressional Review Act to disapprove Environmental Protection Agency authorisations transmitted to Congress as rules in July, and repeal would bar any substantially similar waiver in future.

The harbor craft regulation, adopted in 2009 and amended in 2022, is a significant driver of renewable diesel bunker demand on the US West Coast, mandating R99 or R100 for the state's harbor craft fleet since January 2023 and requiring most vessels to fit diesel particulate filters.

Industry says the filter requirement cannot be met, with no workable marine particulate filter yet designed and the US Coast Guard declining to certify them, according to trade publication The Waterways Journal, and the American Waterways Operators has backed Moreno's resolution, arguing the rule's effects reach beyond California into interstate commerce.

Climate campaign group Pacific Environment, which has led opposition to the resolutions, said in an emailed statement that the vote would kill American competitiveness in shipbuilding.

MPS Egg Farms and Kipster announced Kipster Farm as the winner of the 2026 Indiana Governor's Award for Environmental Excellence, presented by the Indiana Department of Environmental Management (IDEM) in the energy efficiency/renewable resources category. The award recognizes the North Manchester farm for its rooftop solar array and circular-economy operations, developed in partnership with PSG Energy Group and Summit EPC.

"Recognition like the Governor's Award reflects years of investment in doing right by our animals, our community and our environment," said Sam Krouse, co-chief executive officer of MPS Egg Farms. "Partnering with Kipster on this project let us bring that commitment to life in our home state of Indiana."

The farm has a rooftop solar system and operates on circular-economy principles. Hens are fed a diet of upcycled waste streams from human food, agricultural byproducts and other food-industry surplus rather than a conventional corn-soy ration, accounting for more than 7.6 million pounds of circular feed used. Nearly all manure produced on-site is dried using the barns' own ventilation air and sent to partner facility Bionutrients in Wabash, Indiana, for pelletizing into a low-ammonia, organic fertilizer.

The farm's hen houses include indoor areas with natural light and space for hens to perch, roam and dustbathe, as well as outdoor foraging areas. In 2025, Kipster adopted in-ovo sexing technology at the farm to determine the sex of chick embryos before hatching, preventing the industry practice of culling day-old male chicks. Kipster said it is one of a handful of U.S. egg operations using the technology.

"We founded Kipster on the belief that eggs can be produced in ways that place the instincts and needs of chickens at the center, with a lighter footprint and in transparent ways," said Sandra Vijn, Kipster U.S. director. "Being recognized by the State of Indiana for this work is an honor and a sign that sustainable agriculture and a thriving business can go hand in hand."

MPS Egg Farms and Kipster also point to transparency at the site: a North Manchester visitor center, open daily to the public from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., offers a floor-to-ceiling view of the flock, and a livestream lets the public observe the farm at any time. The site has welcomed school groups, university researchers and animal-welfare organizations including the Humane World for Animals and the ASPCA.

This is the latest in a series of honors for the Kipster Farm Project, which has also received the AgriVision Award, the State of Indiana's highest agricultural honor; the Good Egg Award from Compassion in World Farming; and recognition from Fast Company as one of the Top 10 Most Innovative Companies in Agriculture.

title: Curtis Hill: The Seeds of Corporate Politicization Have Already Been Planted
description:
“We live in the world the left created—one in which corporations were turned into instruments of political and cultural power.
What presents itself as even-handedness becomes, in practice, a one-way ratchet: Progressive gains remain institutionalized while the corrective mechanism is dismantled.

text:
“We live in the world the left created—one in which corporations were turned into instruments of political and cultural power. Until those instruments are fully restored to their rightful owners and purpose, the tools of accountability must remain available to those who still believe corporations exist to serve shareholders, not ideological agendas,” writes former Indiana Attorney General Curtis T. Hill, Jr., who now serves with the Free Enterprise Project and Project 21.

In a commentary published at RealClearMarkets, Curtis addresses the misguided proposal by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to extricate itself from shareholder proposal oversight:

For more than a decade, progressive activists have used the very shareholder-proposal process now under review to embed climate mandates, diversity-equity-and-inclusion bureaucracies, viewpoint discrimination, and political advocacy deep inside boardrooms and C-suites….

Now, after that capture has occurred, the sudden shift to a “neutral” regime risks freezing the status quo rather than restoring true neutrality. When the low-cost tool that free-enterprise shareholders have begun using to challenge residual DEI programs, audit political bias, and demand focus on fiduciary duty is removed or heavily restricted, the prior politicization is not reversed. It is locked in. What presents itself as even-handedness becomes, in practice, a one-way ratchet: Progressive gains remain institutionalized while the corrective mechanism is dismantled.

Read Curtis’s entire commentary below.

The Securities and Exchange Commission under Chairman Paul Atkins is right to insist that corporate annual meetings return to their proper purpose: the business of business. Shareholder proposals should not serve as a permanent political soapbox. In a healthy system, management’s duty is to create long-term value for the owners of the company, not to advance the latest ideological fashion. A neutral process that keeps politics out of the proxy is, in principle, a worthy goal.

But principles do not erase history. And history shows that the left has already politicized America’s largest corporations to an extraordinary degree. For more than a decade, progressive activists have used the very shareholder-proposal process now under review to embed climate mandates, diversity-equity-and-inclusion bureaucracies, viewpoint discrimination, and political advocacy deep inside boardrooms and C-suites. Those efforts succeeded. Policies were written. Metrics were adopted. Personnel were hired. Culture was reshaped. The seeds of institutional capture were planted, watered, and allowed to take root. The 2021 Engine No. 1 proxy campaign that ousted Exxon directors over politicized climate strategy stands as an example of how effectively the process was weaponized by progressive shareholder pressure.

Now, after that capture has occurred, the sudden shift to a “neutral” regime risks freezing the status quo rather than restoring true neutrality. When the low-cost tool that free-enterprise shareholders have begun using to challenge residual DEI programs, audit political bias, and demand focus on fiduciary duty is removed or heavily restricted, the prior politicization is not reversed. It is locked in. What presents itself as even-handedness becomes, in practice, a one-way ratchet: Progressive gains remain institutionalized while the corrective mechanism is dismantled.

This is not abstract theory. We have watched companies quiet their public language on DEI and ESG under political pressure while retaining the underlying structures. Board oversight committees for diversity matters persist. Supplier diversity preferences remain in place. Internal metrics and training programs continue under new branding. Rebranding is not renunciation. Temporary silence is not permanent reform. The moment the political winds shift, those same structures stand ready to be reactivated. That is how institutional capture works.

Free-enterprise activists have shown that the same process can be used for accountability rather than ideology. The Free Enterprise Project and allied shareholders have influenced policy clarifications and withdrawals at companies including Prudential, Eli Lilly, and others that had adopted expansive DEI frameworks. These were not symbolic gestures. They forced management to confront whether race- and ideology-based preferences advanced shareholder value or exposed the company to legal and reputational risk. That corrective work remains unfinished.

A genuinely neutral system would have prevented the original politicization. Having failed to do so, it cannot now pretend that ending the game after one side has already scored is fairness.

In a perfect world, shareholder activism beyond the narrow demands of profitability and accountability would be unnecessary. We do not live in that world. We live in the world the left created—one in which corporations were turned into instruments of political and cultural power. Until those instruments are fully restored to their rightful owners and purpose, the tools of accountability must remain available to those who still believe corporations exist to serve shareholders, not ideological agendas.

The SEC’s desire to depoliticize the proxy process is understandable. But timing and residual reality matter. If the Commission proceeds without fully reckoning with the seeds already planted, it will not achieve neutrality. It will achieve permanence—for the very politicization it claims to reject.

America’s capital markets remain the envy of the world because they are grounded in property rights, fiduciary duty, and the pursuit of value. Those foundations are worth defending. They will not defend themselves.

title: Chairman Guthrie Op-Ed: POWER Act puts permitting reform at center of energy affordability
description:
Working families deserve access to abundant and reliable energy, giving them flexibility to invest their hard-earned savings in whatever they deem most important.
Meanwhile, federal and state regulations are forcing reliable power to shut down before replacements are ready, creating a reliability crisis.
“Access to affordable, reliable power will be key as we work to increase domestic manufacturing and power innovative new technologies.
“That is why the POWER Act includes steps to make the permitting process faster and safer.
“The POWER Act cuts through that red tape, helping deliver the energy we need today.”
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – The following op-ed by Congressman Brett Guthrie (KY-02), Chairman of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, appeared in the Washington Times this week.

“Over the past half-decade, energy prices for Americans have risen.

“This has often forced them to make tough decisions about what other goods and services they can afford. This should not be the norm. Working families deserve access to abundant and reliable energy, giving them flexibility to invest their hard-earned savings in whatever they deem most important.

“That goal is achievable, but not through unworkable electricity rate caps, green energy mandates or data center moratoriums, as we have seen proposed by blue-state governors.

“To lower prices while securing our grid, I have released the POWER Act, draft legislation that provides the commonsense permitting reforms needed to bring baseload energy onto our grid while promoting innovation.

“America’s permitting system is broken. Slow, burdensome and unpredictable review processes have produced an unreliable grid and higher costs for consumers. Manufacturers have been forced to contend with longer construction timelines and higher project costs that put the United States at a competitive disadvantage.

“In Democratic-run states, renewable portfolio standards, which are effectively green energy mandates, undermine the reliability of the grid and increase prices. Meanwhile, federal and state regulations are forcing reliable power to shut down before replacements are ready, creating a reliability crisis.

“Layered on top of these challenges, supply chain constraints and equipment backlogs are also slowing the building of industrial projects that America needs to compete.

“The POWER Act addresses these issues by combining into one piece of legislation the commonsense permitting reforms that America needs to speed up the construction of pipelines, power generation and electric transmission.

“This legislation contains three main pillars: producing energy, moving energy and powering industry to build and grow.

“Producing energy domestically is key to securing American energy dominance. From the outset of this Congress, through related hearings and legislation, our House Energy and Commerce Committee has focused on finding ways to generate the reliable, affordable power that our communities need.

“Last winter, we saw the consequences of relying on intermittent sources such as wind and solar, when New England states were forced to burn trash to keep the lights on after renewables failed to provide enough electricity.

“The Power Plant Reliability Act would help address this issue by empowering the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to keep reliable power plants running for up to five years when retiring them would threaten the grid.

“As we work to build our grid and meet America’s growing power demand, driven partly by the need to support data centers, the POWER Act includes the text of the Ratepayer Protection Act. This section builds on the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, under which Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle, xAI and other signers, including utilities and regulators, committed to covering their own data center energy costs.

“While developing the legislation, committee members held hearings and meetings with numerous stakeholders, including the data center industry and Big Tech, state regulators, utilities and community members. Through that work, it has become clear that across the entire industry, one entity is uniquely positioned to stand up for families — the ones paying electricity bills: Congress.

“Modernizing our nation’s infrastructure and building the pipelines needed to carry the oil and natural gas that provide baseload power are critical to lowering prices. That is why this legislation includes the GRID Power Act, which would ensure that grid operators have the tools they need to secure the reliability of the electricity grid in the event of a capacity shortfall.

“Likewise, the Improving Interagency Coordination for Pipeline Reviews Act streamlines permitting for interstate natural gas pipelines at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, supporting the development of dispatchable natural gas to communities across the country.

“Access to affordable, reliable power will be key as we work to increase domestic manufacturing and power innovative new technologies. For too long, burdensome regulations have stood in the way of projects that would help deliver the energy we need.

“That is why the POWER Act includes steps to make the permitting process faster and safer. The bill does this, in part, by streamlining the New Source Review permitting process for companies to upgrade facilities and install modern pollution controls, avoiding delays that would otherwise lead to higher costs.

“Far too often, duplicative reviews slow development while providing no tangible benefits to families. The RED Tape Act ends double reviews of projects by the Environmental Protection Agency if the projects are already vetted under the National Environmental Policy Act.

“Together, these individual measures form the basis for the permitting reform needed to deliver dispatchable baseload power to American families. Permits that take years to acquire slow down development and raise prices for families and businesses.

“The POWER Act cuts through that red tape, helping deliver the energy we need today.”

text:
Elevated Materials, a developer and manufacturer of ultra-thin lithium films for next-generation batteries, has been selected by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) for $50 million in federal funding to support the development of a new $100 million facility in the United States.

The facility is expected to commercialize a new domestic source of ultra-thin lithium-metal films and battery components pre-loaded with extra lithium ions before final cell assembly to replace the lithium lost during initial use. The result is higher-energy, faster-charging batteries. Elevated Materials was one of seven companies selected for a combined $500 million through the DOE’s Battery Materials Processing and Battery Manufacturing Grants program.

“The United States has made advanced battery manufacturing a national priority, and securing a domestic supply of critical materials that significantly increases energy density is central to that effort,” said Jim Cushing, CEO of Santa Clara, Calif.-based Elevated Materials. “We developed this technology in California with support from DOE r&d programs and are proud to have been selected by the Department of Energy to now ramp it up to giga-watt scale.”

The global thin-film battery market is projected to expand beyond $4.5 billion by the mid-2030s, according to Grand View Research. This anticipated growth is driven by high demand for miniaturized power sources. Elevated Materials' proprietary roll-to-roll vacuum deposition platforms produce high-quality ultra-thin lithium metal films that enable next-generation anode architectures across electric vehicles, consumer electronics, defense and aviation applications, and grid-scale energy storage. During the past year, Elevated Materials has shipped more than 250,000 meters of material to customers worldwide.

By expanding U.S. production of these advanced materials, the project advances Department of Energy efforts to strengthen domestic battery manufacturing and reduce reliance on overseas supply chains.

"DOE is taking decisive action to secure the critical supply chains necessary to power our nation," said Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson in a press statement. "These projects underscore DOE’s commitment to driving innovation, reducing reliance on foreign sources and promoting American energy dominance."

name: Detroit Environment
title: Earthshot and the science of positive tipping points: how environmental progress can ...
description:
Our new report applies the science of positive tipping points to the five Earthshot categories – nature, air, oceans, waste and climate – for the first time.
But tipping points science says otherwise.
What is a positive tipping point?
Most environmental interventions assume change is incremental and proportionate: bigger problems require bigger budgets and lead to slower progress.
By using our research to shape how the prize searches for, selects and supports solutions, Earthshot can help trigger positive tipping points to accelerate out of trouble.
text:
It must be tough being a judge on the world’s most prestigious environmental prize: imagine having to choose between an ingenious machine that removes microplastics from a river in Europe, or a company in East Africa that sells clean cookstoves through affordable weekly instalments.

Over the last six months, we have been working with colleagues at Green Futures Solutions at the University of Exeter to make that job a little easier. We have found a way to distinguish between solutions that carry on working as long as people keep putting money into them, and those with “tipping potential” that get better, cheaper and easier to adopt the more successful they are. Our new report applies the science of positive tipping points to the five Earthshot categories – nature, air, oceans, waste and climate – for the first time.

After a northern summer of record-breaking heat, wildfires, floods and a deadly glacier collapse in the Nepal-Tibet border region, it would be easy to conclude the planet is only headed towards collapse. But tipping points science says otherwise. The same dynamic principle that leaves coral reefs and rainforests vulnerable to a relatively abrupt breakdown can also work in our favour – if we know the right levers to pull.

What is a positive tipping point?

Most environmental interventions assume change is incremental and proportionate: bigger problems require bigger budgets and lead to slower progress. But many complex systems we rely on (technologies, markets, societal norms, ecosystems) can shift abruptly once a critical threshold is crossed.

Solar power is a great example. Its cost fell around 90% in a decade because every panel sold stimulated innovation that made the next one cheaper. This attracted more investment, which cut costs again and improved performance. The tipping point happened when self-propelling feedback took over. Clean electricity, our report finds, is now a “master cascade”: as solar and wind have tipped in many markets, clean power can accelerate further progress in electric mobility, residential heating, industrial emissions and air quality.

Our report identifies the potential for such self-propelling feedback across 51 solution areas. Specifically, we identify whether the innovative solution is, or could quickly become, more affordable, accessible, and attractive than the polluting incumbent system it seeks to replace. We have also assigned measurable 2030 targets to each solution area, so progress can be tracked.

Three that could soon tip

Around 2.1 billion people still cook on wood, charcoal or dung and the smoke kills nearly 3 million people a year, including more than 300,000 children under five. Pay-as-you-go finance (borrowed from off-grid solar), turns an unaffordable stove into a small weekly payment. Clean cooking is now close to tipping in several African markets. People switch primarily because it saves them time and money.

Methane is responsible for about 30% of global heating so far, but lasts only around 12 years in the atmosphere. Cutting methane emissions therefore helps cool climate within a decade, rather than a century. A new generation of satellites can now pinpoint methane leaks from individual oil and gas facilities from space, and they are cheap to fix. The gas saved is worth more than the repair.

Inside a well-enforced marine-protected area, where commercial fishing is banned, fish biomass typically reaches four to seven times that of the surrounding waters within five to ten years. Fish spill out across the boundary, nearby fish catches rise, and the fishers who initially opposed the marine-protected area become the constituency demanding more of them. Only around 3% of the ocean is fully protected, but the landmark high seas treaty (itself an Earthshot prizewinner) entered into force this year and aims to protect 30% of the world’s oceans by 2030. Satellites can now monitor some industrial fishing fleets, so enforcement of marine-protected areas is getting easier. The science, the technology and the politics are coming together.

Not everything is about to tip. The biggest brake is investment: Africa receives only 3% of clean energy finance despite holding 60% of the world’s best solar resources. Our report shows where innovative financing could create the conditions to address these barriers, and highlights how the current investment gaps in adaptation financing can be closed.

By using our research to shape how the prize searches for, selects and supports solutions, Earthshot can help trigger positive tipping points to accelerate out of trouble.

text:
Deb Haaland, the former U.S. Interior secretary and New Mexico’s Democratic gubernatorial nominee, on Thursday said if elected she would sign an executive order immediately upon taking office to pause all new large-scale data center proposals while state lawmakers craft guidelines for such developments.

Several lawmakers announced plans in recent months to introduce such a moratorium, amid increasing public consternation about data centers, and as various local governments also grapple with the issue.

Haaland said she hopes that any guardrails the Legislature proposes in next year’s legislative session include specific requirements, including: prohibiting non-disclosure agreements; requiring that developers build their own renewable energy infrastructure; requiring closed-loop cooling systems; prioritizing hiring New Mexicans for union jobs; mandating compliance with the state’s clean-energy goals; adhering to high standards for light pollution, noise and more; and imposing decommission bonds similar to those in the oil and gas industry.

Developers must exceed those standards to qualify for incentives from state business programs, she said.

“Big tech’s mantra may be ‘move fast and break things,’ but here in New Mexico, we do things our way,” Haaland told reporters during a news conference at the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center in Albuquerque. “The lack of transparency, the NDAs and backroom deals will never build trust with New Mexico communities.”

She said she remains open to working with a diverse range of industries seeking to do business in the state, but wants to first establish guardrails to protect New Mexico’s air, land and water.

“I want to be crystal clear that New Mexico is open for business,” she said. “These guidelines will provide more predictability and certainty and will help businesses be more responsible, and that’s good for everyone.”

Haaland cited her time as Interior secretary under the Biden administration and said she oversaw the investment of more than $10 billion in statewide infrastructure, conservation and clean energy projects.

Her announcement comes as her latest campaign finance reports show she’s received donations from Oracle, one of the tech companies behind the controversial Project Jupiter data center in Doña Ana County, and its CEO.

During the news conference, Haaland said that campaigning for office is excessively expensive work and said she remained committed to holding industry leaders to account, even if they donate to her campaign.

New Mexico State Ethics Commission says Oracle’s $3.4M Project Jupiter ads sought to sway permitting

“I believe that I can walk and chew gum at the same time,” she said.

When asked how she would apply the proposed guardrails to data center developments that finish construction before New Mexico elects a new governor, she said it would be “embedded into any rulemaking that the Legislature decides to work up.”

Haaland’s plan also calls for data center developments to use renewable energy. Developers across the nation have increasingly proposed building small nuclear reactors on-site to power their data centers. Haaland said she would prefer other renewable energy sources, such as solar, wind and geothermal power.

“The majority of New Mexicans that I speak with are not in favor of nuclear anything,” she said. “We have all the sun, we have all the wind, we have all the geothermal.”

The state House Democratic Caucus in a Thursday statement responding to Haaland’s plan said that no industry should have “free rein in our state.”

“Over the past several months, members of the House Democratic caucus have been working diligently on a range of legislation for the 2027 session to address these concerns,” the statement said. “New Mexicans deserve clean and safe water, affordable utility bills, and assurance that if data centers set up shop here, they must benefit our communities and provide good paying union jobs.”

A spokesperson for Gregg Hull, the former Rio Rancho mayor running as the Republican nominee for governor, told Source NM that Hull believes a moratorium “signals to businesses that New Mexico is closed for business” and referred to Hull’s prior comments on the matter.

Hull previously said in a statement to Source NM that he doesn’t “support a blank check, either.”

“Data centers need to be sited responsibly — with real accountability for water use, energy impact, and community input and with siting decisions driven by local infrastructure capacity, not just available land,” he said at the time. “As governor, I’d rather fix the guardrails than shut the door on an entire industry.”

title: Korean battery makers under Trump whims – from EV retreat to datacenters | Aju Press
description:
The reversal has hit a string of multibillion-dollar ventures involving LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI.
In Glendale, Kentucky, about 1,500 workers were laid off in December at the $5.8 billion battery complex originally built by Ford and SK On.
U.S. EV sales fell 20.5 percent from a year earlier to 247,226 vehicles in the second quarter, according to Cox Automotive.
Ford also terminated a large battery-supply agreement with LG Energy Solution as it shifted capital away from some EV programs.
SK On, meanwhile, has been reviewing ways to redirect underused U.S. production capacity as EV demand softens.
text:
SEOUL, September 17 (AJP) - U.S. President Donald Trump's retreat from Biden-era electric-vehicle policies has upended the American growth plans of South Korean battery makers, leaving factories built for an EV boom idled, scaled back or searching for a new purpose.

Now, some are finding one in the power-hungry data-center boom.

Canceled U.S. EV and battery projects between January 2025 and August this year had promised about 27,000 jobs, according to a Reuters analysis of Atlas Public Policy data. About four-fifths of the canceled investment was in Republican-leaning states.

The reversal has hit a string of multibillion-dollar ventures involving LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI.

Ultium Cells, the $2.3 billion battery plant in Lordstown, Ohio, owned by General Motors and LG Energy Solution, halted production in January after weakening EV demand and initially placed about 480 workers on indefinite layoff.

Cell production resumed in mid-August, bringing back about 700 workers, but roughly 600 remained on indefinite layoff, the company told Reuters.

In Glendale, Kentucky, about 1,500 workers were laid off in December at the $5.8 billion battery complex originally built by Ford and SK On. The project had once been pitched as creating about 5,000 jobs.

Part of the roughly $6 billion, 2,800-job battery complex planned by Stellantis and Samsung SDI in Kokomo, Indiana, has also stalled.

The retrenchment accelerated after the $7,500 federal EV purchase tax credit expired on Sept. 30, 2025, following legislation backed by Trump and congressional Republicans.

The administration also eased vehicle-emissions rules and other policies that had supported EV adoption. Automakers have cited those policy changes, together with softer-than-expected consumer demand, in reassessing EV investment. "Electric cars are fine, but not everyone should be forced to own one," Trump wrote on Truth Social in July 2025, calling what he described as the EV mandate "ridiculous."

U.S. EV sales fell 20.5 percent from a year earlier to 247,226 vehicles in the second quarter, according to Cox Automotive. EVs accounted for about 5.8 percent of total new-vehicle sales, down sharply from a record 10.6 percent in the third quarter of 2025, when buyers rushed to qualify for expiring incentives.

Ford has been among the most aggressive in resetting its EV ambitions.

The automaker booked a $19.5 billion writedown in December, ended plans for several electric models and dissolved its battery joint venture with SK On. Ford also terminated a large battery-supply agreement with LG Energy Solution as it shifted capital away from some EV programs.

Its unopened Tennessee assembly plant, once intended to build electric pickups, is being redirected toward gasoline-powered trucks.

But the battery factories built to power cars are not necessarily being abandoned. Increasingly, they are being retooled to power something else: artificial intelligence.

The explosive construction of data centers is creating a new market for energy-storage systems, or ESS, which absorb electricity and release it when grids or facilities need additional power.

Ford plans to hire about 2,100 workers at its Glendale battery complex from late 2027 to produce energy-storage batteries — less than half the workforce originally projected for the site when it was built around EV demand.

LG Energy Solution is making a similar pivot.

The company is expanding lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery production for stationary storage and aims to have more than 50 gigawatt-hours of ESS production capacity across North America by the end of this year. Its North American network includes plants in Michigan and Ontario as well as joint-venture facilities in Ohio and Tennessee.

Samsung SDI is also pushing deeper into storage.

Its StarPlus Energy venture in Indiana is producing batteries for U.S. ESS contracts, and the company has signed large supply deals aimed at the North American market. Samsung SDI said in August that another Indiana plant would also be used for energy-storage batteries as market demand changes.

SK On, meanwhile, has been reviewing ways to redirect underused U.S. production capacity as EV demand softens.

The shift toward storage is already showing up in Korean battery makers' earnings.

All three major Korean battery companies returned to operating profit in the second quarter, though for different reasons. Samsung SDI posted a 203.8 billion won operating profit, its first in seven quarters, with demand for batteries used in energy storage and AI-related backup-power applications helping the rebound. LG Energy Solution posted a 113.3 billion won operating profit as ESS revenue surged.

LG Energy Solution’s underlying business, however, remained in the red. Excluding 241 billion won in U.S. production tax credits, it recorded an operating loss of about 127.7 billion won.

SK On also returned to profit after seven quarters, helped by increased Asian battery sales, customer compensation and U.S. production incentives rather than storage alone.

The new market offers relief, but not a full replacement for the EV boom the plants were designed to serve.

Converting battery lines can take months or years because stationary-storage batteries often use different chemistries and specifications.

Storage demand is also not expected to absorb all of the EV capacity now sitting idle or underused.

For Korean battery makers, the U.S. bet has therefore changed more quickly than the factories themselves.

Plants built to ride America's EV transition are being forced to chase its next power-hungry growth engine — the data centers feeding the artificial-intelligence boom.

"Because subsidies expired on Sept. 30, 2025, pull-forward demand concentrated sales between July and September, meaning this year's third quarter will face a much steeper year-on-year comparison," said Kim Hyun-soo, an analyst at Hana Securities.

"From October, the base effect eases, making a return to year-on-year growth likely."

AJP Takeaways

- Canceled U.S. EV and battery projects between January 2025 and August 2026 had promised about 27,000 jobs, according to a Reuters analysis of Atlas Public Policy data. About four-fifths of canceled investment was in Republican-leaning states.

- U.S. facilities involving LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI have been idled, scaled back or reworked as EV demand weakened following the expiry of the $7,500 federal tax credit.

- Korean battery makers are increasingly redirecting U.S. capacity toward energy-storage batteries serving utilities and the fast-growing AI and data-center market. Ford plans to hire 2,100 workers for storage-battery production at its Glendale, Kentucky, complex from late 2027.

title: Powering Progress: Public-Private Partnerships - Bipartisan Policy Center
description:
Public-private partnerships are a critical mechanism for delivering infrastructure and innovation projects that are the backbone of the U.S. economy.
This article lays out what public-private partnerships are, why they can be useful, and why they matter now.
Why Are Public-Private Partnerships Needed?
P3s benefit the private sector by transforming volatile, high-cost infrastructure projects into stable, long-term commercial investments.
Why Do Public-Private Partnerships Matter Now?
text:
Public-private partnerships are a critical mechanism for delivering infrastructure and innovation projects that are the backbone of the U.S. economy. As the nation confronts mounting infrastructure needs and a rapidly evolving technological landscape, these partnerships offer a proven way to align public objectives with private capability, helping critical projects move from concept to completion. By mobilizing private capital and expertise, government can accelerate infrastructure projects—from power generation and transmission to roads and bridges—and advance capital-intensive projects that might otherwise stall if government financed and built them alone. This article lays out what public-private partnerships are, why they can be useful, and why they matter now.

What Is a Public-Private Partnership?

A public-private partnership—often shortened to P3 or PPP—in the context of infrastructure projects is a long-term arrangement in which a government agency and a private company share the work, financing, and risk of delivering an asset or service that is for public use or benefit. The public partner might be a city, state, or federal agency; the private partner might be a single firm or a consortium assembled for the project.

What sets a P3 project apart is its structure. In traditional financing and development for a project to benefit the public, a government entity hires a contractor (or directs public employees) to build something, pays the costs for the development project with public funds, and then owns and operates it. At the other end of the spectrum, a project or facility to benefit the public might be financed, built, and owned by a private entity.

A P3 project occupies the middle ground. The private party might design, build, finance, operate, and maintain the asset under a contract that can run for decades, while a government entity might maintain ownership and ultimate accountability. Because the private partner finances the project, P3s avoid the need for federal, state, or local governments to appropriate public funds or incur debt to finance and build the project. In addition, the private partner can absorb most or all of the financial risks of the project—including cost overruns and the costs of delays, project redesigns, usage, revenue, and performance shortfalls.

Why Are Public-Private Partnerships Needed?

When applied to energy, infrastructure, and innovation, P3s can serve as effective accelerators for the following reasons.

Access to capital. Drawing on private capital eases pressure on public budgets, allowing projects to move forward more quickly, even during times of significantly constrained government budgets. While avoiding the need for the large amount of taxpayer funds needed to build a major project, P3 projects can sometimes benefit from access to preferential loan rates from government entities.

Innovation. P3s can help the public sector benefit from the latest private-sector innovations without duplicating R&D efforts.

Talent. The private sector can bring a highly skilled workforce to the table, bypassing the government’s sometimes rigid pay scales, hiring practices, and slow recruitment processes.

Life-cycle accountability. When private entities design, build, operate, and maintain a project, they are incentivized to evaluate and internalize the full life-cycle cost and have an incentive to build well upfront.

P3s benefit the private sector by transforming volatile, high-cost infrastructure projects into stable, long-term commercial investments. Partnering with the public sector can enable risk sharing, facilitate permitting, and provide guaranteed revenue streams that extend over decades.

Why Do Public-Private Partnerships Matter Now?

The United States faces a converging set of energy, infrastructure, and innovation challenges that likely exceed the capacity of either the public or private sector to address alone. Rapid electricity load growth driven by electrification, data centers, and advanced manufacturing is straining an aging grid that requires large-scale expansion, modernization, and faster interconnection. Transportation systems face pressures from new technologies such as driverless cars while aging road and rail infrastructure assets must compete for scarce public dollars. Across the energy, transportation, and technology sectors, deploying next-generation technologies, upgrading legacy infrastructure, and innovating artificial intelligence require substantial upfront capital and long development timelines.

What’s Next?

P3s are a long-standing, common way of advancing technology and building essential infrastructure. This article is the first in a series that delves into P3s and their significance. Forthcoming articles in this series will examine how these partnerships work in three critical areas shaping economic growth and competitiveness. The second article will focus on transportation, examining the use of P3s to finance, build, and operate critical infrastructure while balancing efficiency, risk allocation, and public value. The third will focus on successful transmission P3s, highlighting projects and partnership structures that have expanded grid infrastructure, improved reliability, and mobilized investment to meet growing electricity demand. The final article will explore the role of P3s in advancing AI innovation, focusing on how governments and private firms can collaborate to accelerate technological development.

text:
Today, Congresswoman Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), joined members of Congress and labor and environmental advocates in front of the U.S. Capitol to speak out against the Trump administration’s continued attacks on offshore wind. Pingree joined Representatives Deborah Ross (D-N.C.), Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.) and Senator Ed Markey (D-Mass.)—along with Kendall Martin, General Vice President of Ironworkers International, and Bob Keefe, Executive Director of E2 | Economy+Environment—to call attention to the lack of accountability around the corrupt, taxpayer-funded offshore wind buyout deals, which now cover 12 offshore wind leases and five developers. Since March, the Department of the Interior has made unprecedented use of the Treasury Department’s Judgment Fund to pay developers nearly $4 billion in taxpayer funds to vacate their offshore wind leases.

“The Trump administration is spending nearly $4 billion in taxpayer funds to cancel 12 offshore wind leases at the same time when Americans' utility bills are rising. Their priorities are completely out of whack," said Congresswoman Chellie Pingree (ME-01). “As Ranking Member of the Interior and Environment Appropriations Subcommittee, I take Congress’s power of the purse seriously. Taxpayers deserve to know who authorized these buyouts, how they were valued, and why the Judgment Fund was used. We need transparency, accountability, and more affordable, reliable domestic energy—not dirty deals that force taxpayers to pay for less of it.”

President Trump continues to wage his war on offshore wind amid rising electricity demand and skyrocketing energy bills. These cancellations jeopardize clean energy projects that would have delivered affordable, reliable energy to millions of U.S. households and businesses and hobble industries that create thousands of good-paying jobs across the country.

To date, the administration has bought out twelve offshore wind leases, including planned projects off the coasts of Maine, New York, New Jersey, California, North Carolina, and Massachusetts. Cancelling these leases takes away planned domestic power generation and hinders grid diversification, causing real reliability risks and higher energy bills for millions.

“I’ve seen firsthand what offshore wind and renewable energy can do for our communities. They can lower costs, provide new sources of power to our homes and businesses, and create good-paying jobs. My home state of North Carolina has been a long time leader in clean energy, including offshore wind," said Congresswoman Deborah Ross (NC-02). “The cancelled projects would have created thousands of good-paying jobs and powered over 300,000 homes. This is happening when we are already experiencing record-high electricity prices across our state. [...] President Trump and the Department of Energy put their political agenda ahead of North Carolina's economic and energy needs. Families cannot afford to pay the price for that.”

“What is so outrageous about these buyouts that are now totaling almost $4 billion of taxpayer money that’s just been lit on fire is that we’re going through a time when families are struggling," said Congressman Jared Huffman (CA-02). “We’ve got this industry ready to make major investments in coastal communities that will not only create jobs but will provide cheap and reliable clean power that will bring electric rates down. This is exactly what we need at this time.”

The EPA also set its intention to repeal any remaining carbon emissions rules, too.
That would include any new natural gas power plants, such as the 1,500 megawatt power plant proposed for rural Mitchell County, south of Albany.
text:
The federal Environmental Protection Agency has rolled back rules restricting climate warming emissions at electrical power plants, including those in Georgia.

The rules the EPA ended this week date from the Biden administration and would have required coal and natural gas-fired power plants to restrict carbon emissions starting in 2030.

That was about the same time Georgia Power had planned to shutter its two largest coal plants — Plant Bowen, which is north of Atlanta, and Plant Scherer, just north of Macon. But now with the data center boom, Georgia Power is keeping the plants running. With the help of a third coal plant over the border in Alabama, Georgia Power hopes to meet fully 70% of the data center demand.

Plant Scherer is on the Ocmulgee River, in the Altamaha River watershed. Altamaha Riverkeeper Fletcher Sams said the decision is a greenlight for unchecked pollution.

“This rollback is going to allow Georgia Power to run these aging antique coal plants indefinitely,” he said.

Plant Bowen’s units all came online in the 1970s. Plant Scherer’s went online in the ’80s. The Trump administration is fighting to keep even older coal plants up and running.

Last year, the two Georgia plants produced about 22 million tons of carbon dioxide, putting them near the top for greenhouse gas pollution among over 1,000 U.S. power plants and accounting for just under half of the carbon emissions of Georgia Power’s entire generation fleet.

Sams points to other pollutants in coal plant emissions as things Georgians will still be living with once the looser carbon rules keep the coal plants online rather than replacing them with cleaner combined cycle natural gas turbines.

“It’s hard to run a coal plant clean,” he said. “You have the mercury emissions and heavy metal emissions coming out of the stack that wouldn’t be coming out with the combined cycle turbines.”

Sams says much of that pollution will still end up in the state’s streams and rivers. Other things, such as particulate emissions, will continue to contribute to ground-level ozone and health conditions that come with it, such as asthma.

A 2023 study by a host of universities which included Georgia Tech suggested those emissions contributed to 500,000 excess deaths over 20 years. Plant Bowen was found to be the second most deadly power plant in the study. Bowen was thought to be responsible for deaths as far away as New York.

Meanwhile, the EPA in its announcement of the rule change said it now expects coal use to increase by a factor of 10. The EPA also set its intention to repeal any remaining carbon emissions rules, too. That would include any new natural gas power plants, such as the 1,500 megawatt power plant proposed for rural Mitchell County, south of Albany. Resident Lauren Dorminey has been organizing political opposition for months to the project pursued by Florida based NextEra Energy.

“I cannot trust energy industries who benefit by the millions from regulatory rollbacks,” Dorminey said. “Air, along with water, are two of our major concerns. So of course this is alarming.”

Maggie Shober, research director with the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, also blasted the rollback.

“Through this action, the administration once again prioritizes short-term gains for wealthy donors over the lives and livelihoods of the American people,” Shober said. “Coal and gas are fossils, and the dinosaurs are in charge.”

Shober pointed to the effects of Hurricane Helene as a piece of the fallout from continued greenhouse emissions.

Gudrun Thompson, Energy Program Leader for the Southern Environmental Law Center, called the rule rollback a “gift to polluters.”

“In the South, climate pollution is harming our neighbors and the places we love,” Thompson said. “With power plants spewing over a quarter of the carbon pollution in the U.S., this rollback not only violates the law, it defies common sense.”

In an emailed comment, a Georgia Power representative said the company is reviewing the EPA’s actions on greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act and will “continue to constructively engage with our state public service commissions and environmental regulators to serve customers with clean, safe, reliable, and affordable energy.”

The EPA rule change will almost certainly face court challenges.

title: Editorial: Power down regulations to power up debate - Sacramento Bee
authors: Las Vegas Review-Journal, Las Vegas Review-Journal, Ronaldo Schemidt
description:
The agency is rolling back greenhouse gas requirements on power plants that the Biden administration enacted.
If left in place, these regulations would likely have shut down most coal power plants by 2040.
In 2025, coal power accounted for almost 17 percent of the country's power, the third highest source.
Coal is also more useful than solar power because coal power plants can produce power when the sun isn't shining.
While the effects won't be instantaneous, these rules set the stage for lower power prices than if the previous regulations had remained.
text:
A major change by the Trump administration will reduce future power prices around the country. Unfortunately, it took a unilateral act of the executive branch rather than an act of Congress.

On Monday, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced sweeping changes to the U.S. power sector. The agency is rolling back greenhouse gas requirements on power plants that the Biden administration enacted. If left in place, these regulations would likely have shut down most coal power plants by 2040. They were part of the Biden administration's expensive war on fossil fuels.

Nevada generally relies on natural gas to provide reliable power, but coal remains a vital part of the country's power system. In 2025, coal power accounted for almost 17 percent of the country's power, the third highest source. The top two were natural gas, at 40.8 percent, and nuclear at 17.7 percent. In contrast, solar energy provided 6.7 percent. Coal is also more useful than solar power because coal power plants can produce power when the sun isn't shining.

As data centers demand ever more power, there is a great need for reliable sources of it. This move by the Trump administration removes a costly roadblock to meeting that demand. The EPA estimates it will save $310 billion. It also wants to rescind "every remaining greenhouse gas standard for the power sector," according to a release.

Zeldin pointed out that both "the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy." In contrast, this move will give Americans "a decrease in electricity prices."

This is an important example of Trump keeping his pledge to "unleash American energy," as the White House puts it. While the effects won't be instantaneous, these rules set the stage for lower power prices than if the previous regulations had remained.

Yet, a move this consequential has received comparatively little attention. That isn't because electricity is a niche issue. It's a foundational part of the modern world we take for granted.

It's because both the initial Biden administration change and this reversal came via regulations, not through congressional legislation. Any federal dictate this broad should be debated and passed by Congress. The House and Senate should have to approve it and the president should sign or veto the measure. This would likely produce a compromise more in line with the American public - and allow voters to hold elected officials accountable for major policy changes.

Governance by regulations short circuits important public debate on major policy issues. It's one reason the country remains so divided.

title: Goodlander, Harrigan Launch Bipartisan Hydropower Caucus to Lower Energy Costs
description:
The caucus will support and advocate for America’s first renewable energy resource and keep hydropower at the center of congressional work to lower energy costs, strengthen grid reliability, create jobs, and expand American energy production.
“Hydropower is at the heart of lowering energy costs for hardworking Granite Staters and making America the world’s clean energy superpower,” said Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander.
“We applaud Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander’s leadership in launching the Hydropower Caucus and elevating the role of America’s first renewable energy resource.
“NHA applauds Representatives Goodlander and Harrigan for launching the bipartisan Hydropower Caucus.
Listening to New Hampshire hydropower leaders: On National Hydropower Day, Goodlander visited Great River Hydro’s Vernon Station in Hinsdaleto see how New Hampshire hydropower is delivering affordable, reliable power.
text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander (NH-02) and Congressman Pat Harrigan (NC-10) launched the bipartisan Hydropower Caucus, a new forum to bring together Members of Congress with hydropower and marine energy experts across federal agencies, industry, and stakeholder organizations.

The caucus will support and advocate for America’s first renewable energy resource and keep hydropower at the center of congressional work to lower energy costs, strengthen grid reliability, create jobs, and expand American energy production.

“Hydropower is at the heart of lowering energy costs for hardworking Granite Staters and making America the world’s clean energy superpower,” said Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander. “For generations, hydropower has delivered reliable, homegrown energy to communities across New Hampshire and our country. Our bipartisan caucus will bring together the people with the expertise and ideas we need to cut red tape, invest in innovation, and get more affordable American energy online. I’m proud to lead this effort with Congressman Harrigan, and I will keep working across the aisle to lower costs and build an energy future that works for the people we serve.”

“We are asking more of our electric grid every year, while some of the most reliable power in the country is already being generated by infrastructure we built generations ago,” said Congressman Pat Harrigan. “Hydropower works, it’s American, and there is no good reason outdated permitting and licensing should stand in the way of getting more out of it. The Hydropower Caucus gives us a bipartisan forum to work through those barriers, bring the people who actually build and operate these systems to the table, and make sure this proven source of American energy has a much bigger role in meeting the demand ahead.”

The Hydropower Caucus will serve as a venue to inform and educate Members of Congress and their staff and connect them with hydropower and marine energy subject matter experts at federal agencies, in industry, and at related stakeholder organizations. It will convene discussions on the issues facing hydropower and marine energy, including permitting and licensing reform, federal incentive programs, tax policy, research, development, and deployment.

“Hydropower is the nation’s longest tenured electricity generator, providing clean, reliable, and affordable power to homes and businesses for over a century. Hydropower was the backbone of the industrial revolution and, with proper stewardship, will see us through the information age as well. Hydropower has always benefited from strong bipartisan support as a result, which is why we are so proud that the Granite State’s own Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander (D-NH) has stepped forward to co-chair the Congressional Hydropower Caucus with Representative Pat Harrigan of North Carolina (R). New Hampshire, New England, and the Nation as a whole will benefit from Congresswoman Goodlander’s leadership, ensuring hydropower remains a core component of our domestic energy supply deep into the 21st century,” said Brandon Kibbe, Vice President of External Affairs for Great River Hydro.

“We applaud Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander’s leadership in launching the Hydropower Caucus and elevating the role of America’s first renewable energy resource. This caucus will provide an important forum for educating policymakers and advancing thoughtful solutions on licensing, permitting, tax policy, and other issues that are critical to ensuring hydropower continues to deliver reliable, affordable, and carbon-free electricity for New Hampshire and the nation,” said Bob King, President of the Granite State Hydropower Association.

“NHA applauds Representatives Goodlander and Harrigan for launching the bipartisan Hydropower Caucus. Hydropower is America’s first renewable energy resource, operating in 48 states and providing reliable power to nearly 30 million Americans. Yet too few people understand its benefits and the policy challenges it faces. The Hydropower Caucus can help change that by educating lawmakers and stakeholders about the many ways hydropower supports our communities—not only through affordable, reliable electricity, but also through irrigation, flood control, recreation, and good-paying jobs. We thank Representatives Goodlander and Harrigan for their leadership in advancing this important effort,” said Matthew Allen, Senior Director of Legislative Affairs for the National Hydropower Association.

ADDITIONAL BACKGROUND:

Goodlander has made expanding affordable, reliable hydropower and lowering energy costs a central part of her work in Congress:

Cutting red tape to unlock low-cost hydropower: In July, Goodlander introduced legislation alongside Rep. Carol Miller (R-WV), Sen. Steve Daines (R-MT), and Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-NH) making it easier to get reliable, low-cost hydropower projects built faster at existing Army Corps of Engineers dams.

Investing in existing hydropower and healthy rivers: Goodlander helped introduce the bipartisan Maintaining and Enhancing Hydroelectricity and River Restoration Act, H.R. 2160, to extend a 30 percent investment tax credit through 2031 for upgrades at existing hydroelectric facilities, environmental improvements, and removal of obsolete river barriers.

Listening to New Hampshire hydropower leaders: On National Hydropower Day, Goodlander visited Great River Hydro’s Vernon Station in Hinsdaleto see how New Hampshire hydropower is delivering affordable, reliable power. She also visited Essex Hydro Associates in Penacook and met with Granite State Hydropower Association leaders.

Lowering energy bills: Goodlander is helping to lead a number of bipartisan bills designed to bring down energy costs, including the bipartisan Weatherization Enhancement and Readiness Act, to expand support for home energy-efficiency upgrades and help households save money on utility bills while making homes safer and healthier. She has also championed the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), a mission-critical program for millions of American families. Goodlander joined the New Hampshire delegation in opposing the Trump administration’s attempt to terminate New Hampshire’s $43.5 million Solar for All grant, which would have supported community energy projects and reduced utility bills for low-income households by 20 percent or more.

Cracking down on runaway utility profiteering: Goodlander helped introduce the Lowering Utility Bills Act, legislation to rein in excessive profits by investor-owned electric utilities, gas utilities, and transmission providers by requiring them to use the lowest return on equity within an established range of reasonableness when setting rates. Goodlander is leading the charge to hold Liberty Utilities accountable after the company refused to serve natural gas customers in New Hampshire’s Lakes Region, causing delays and higher costs for new homes in communities already struggling with the housing crisis. She also worked alongside New Hampshire’s Office of the Consumer Advocate to take on Eversource when the utility proposed a 43.4% rate hike, and pressed the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to crack down on utilities’ attempts to overcharge customers on their electric bills.

description:
